speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $745,000,000 ANNOUNCEMENT AS TO OVER-SUBSCRIPTION ON OPENING DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know the house will be happy to learn of the successful result of our 1950 refunding loan offering. Hon. members will recall that the loan was offered for the purpose of paying off two Government of Canada issues which had been called for payment on June 1 and June 15 respectively, and was for a total amount of $745 million. The loan was offered in two maturities, an eighteen year 2f per cent bond and a four and a half year 2 per cent bond, and I reserved the right to close the books at any time and to determine the amount of bonds to be allotted in each maturity.
The books of the loan were opened at 9 a.m. this morning and were closed at
9.01	a.m. At that time the loan was very heavily over-subscribed, and allotments of both long term and short term bonds have to be substantially less than the subscriptions. The Bank of Canada will be advising primary distributors by overnight telegram tonight as to the portion of their orders which will be filled. As between the long term and short term issues, the loan has been allotted as follows; $350 million in the 2f per cent eighteen year bonds and $395 million in the 2 per cent four and a half year bonds.
This issue represents the largest offering the government has ever made under ordinary peacetime conditions. Its long term portion represents the first offering of ordinary market bonds we have made to the general public since the ninth victory loan bonds were offered in the fall of 1945. Therefore I think we may all take pride in the remarkable success of this loan flotation. The enthusiastic and general response of investors throughout the country provides substantial evidence of prosperous conditions and of confidence in the future of the country. In conclusion I wish to thank the investment dealers and banks whose efforts contributed to the successful placing of the bonds with investors in all parts of the country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 177, to amend the Income Tax Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have only a word to say in connection with this bill. I regret that it was found necessary to have it run to such length, but there are two or three reasons for that. There are relatively few changes involving important questions of principle, such as the new provisions with respect to surpluses of closely held companies, some provisions respecting charitable corporations, and the like. However, as the house will appreciate, when changes of that kind are introduced it is necessary to make a number of consequential amendments in other sections of the act.
Income Tax Act
As the house will recall, in 1948 we passed a completely new Income Tax Act, and as a result of experience over the last year it has been found desirable to make some changes and improvements in various sections of it. Moreover, because of the virtual elimination of ministerial discretion in the Income Tax Act it has become necessary to spell out in a great deal more detail a number of its provisions. It is for these reasons that the amending act runs to such length.
The house will recall that I introduced it a week or ten days ago, and it has been allowed to stand during that period in order that hon. members might have an opportunity of examining its provisions, and also in order that we might receive criticism and suggestions from those outside the house who may be interested in its provisions. I am glad to say that we have received a number of very helpful and constructive suggestions from the Canadian Tax Foundation, and others; and when we are in committee I shall have some amendments to offer to the sections as they now stand which I think will further improve the act. I hope we may be able to proceed to consideration of the bill in committee at a reasonably early hour.

Mr. Speaker, I believe one can be thankful for certain forward steps indicated in this bill amending the Income Tax Act. I think there has been a definite attempt to deal with the question of surpluses. I welcome one thing in that connection, that instead of the old-fashioned remedy of pains and penalties, the new clauses turn to the much more helpful area of incentive. In other words, companies are given an incentive to come in and pay the taxes which are indicated. Without labouring the point at the moment I think it is permissible to ask-and it will be asked in committee-why this is limited only to private companies; but on that I shall say no more at the moment.	[DOT]
The other thing one welcomes-and perhaps we on this side may try to arrogate to ourselves a little credit for this-is that the provisions for assisting small companies, which last autumn we felt had been so much tied up by the then legislation, have been relaxed, and I hope in a constructive way.
Having said those things, of course, one must not forget to remind the house that we still have the heavy burden of double taxation. A beginning was made to lighten it; nevertheless it has been lightened very little. One thing of which we shall all be glad is that section 6 disappears-that is, the section
55946-165i

Income Tax Act
which enabled government officials to step in and tell companies what they were to do with their surplus.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Section 9, subsection 6.

Section 9. The legislation before us encourages one to hope that the time may come when even section 126, I think it is, may be eliminated. Under this section a discretion is still reserved in the department to tell a man he must pay more taxes, even when he has complied with the law in every way and has paid his full taxes. We feel that this is a scandalous provision.
I was glad to hear the minister say that ministerial discretions were being eliminated. We shall all rejoice when that is done. After all, we do exist as a civilization probably mainly because of the rule of law. This section 126 seems to be a contravention of that basic principle in our lives.
I think, Mr. Speaker, the other points I might mention are details which could be dealt with in committee.

There are one or two things I should like to say before the bill goes to the committee. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has referred to the fact that there was a complete revision of the act in 1948. The members who were in the house at that time will recall that only two days, or parts of two days, were spent in the banking and commerce committee in a detailed review of that long and important measure. I believe it will be a matter of general regret, Mr. Speaker, that it has been found necessary now to undertake two quite substantial revisions of that important legislation within the last two years. After all, the bill itself was a bill extending to eighty-eight pages. In Bill No. 176, at the second session of this parliament in 1949, we had a measure extending to forty-one pages. In Bill No. 177, now before the house, we have further amendments extending to twenty-nine pages.
While the house will always be glad of an opportunity to remedy weaknesses or injustices in the act, I think this experience does point to the fact that we must take greater care in this house in connection with our taxing legislation. If I may suggest it, when major measures of this kind come before the house, such as the one in 1948, more time should be spent on them in the proper committee.
There is a second regret that I am quite certain will be shared by all members of the house who have made any effort to read and digest the terms of this bill. The regret was expressed last November and December, sir, during the debate on Bill No. 176 of that
CMr. Macdonnell (Greenwood).]
session. It is that our taxing statutes, particularly the Income Tax Act, are constantly becoming couched in more and more abstruse language. If there is one feature of taxing legislation that is more objectionable than another, it is when its provisions defy clear understanding and relatively simple reading. I grant you that if we are to deal with situations in great detail in our taxing acts we are going to have long acts with very detailed provisions, but I submit that we should follow that good axiom that taxing legislation should be written in as clear, simple and understandable terms as possible. Departures from the observance of that axiom ought not to be tolerated by the house if they can possibly be prevented.
Attention was drawn last fall to the very complicated and involved terms of Bill No. 176. I am certain, sir, that those members of the house who have taken the trouble to read the bill before us, and have tried to understand its provisions, will share the regret that it has not been found possible by the draftsmen to couch the terms of the bill in simple, understandable language. It is an extremely abstruse and complicated bill.
In conclusion, sir-because I appreciate there will need to be some time spent in the committee on the detailed clauses of the bill-I mention my disappointment that there are not certain provisions to be found in the bill which some of us had hoped to see in it. In the first place, notwithstanding what the minister had to say on the subject in his budget speech, some of us still hoped that the minister would see fit to introduce some provisions which would dispel the fear that does exist on a substantial scale today that capital gains are in danger of taxation. In his budget speech the minister indicated that he did not think it was possible to go any further in defining income under the act, in order to make it quite clear it is not intended to tax capital gains. The language used in certain recent court decisions, it seems to me, makes it desirable, if not imperative, to clarify the legislation, and a provision of that kind ought to be introduced. I express my regret that such a clarifying provision is not to be found in this bill.
One further matter-and this is not new on my part, because I have raised the point in several previous sessions-I regret that the minister has not seen fit to introduce amendments to section 26 of the act. This section defines the "extraordinary medical expenses" which the taxpayer may deduct to the extent that those expenses exceed four per cent of his income. The minister has not seen fit to propose the elimination of two

obvious anomalies and discriminations. In the first place, while the section permits the inclusion within the definition of "extraordinary medical expenses" of aids to hearing or aids to cripples, no inclusion is offered of aids to sight. I submit, Mr. Speaker, there is no principle which at the one time justifies the inclusion within this definition of aids to hearing or aids to walking, and at the same time excludes aids to seeing. I urge that the expenditure on eyeglasses ought to be included within the definition of extraordinary medical expenses.
The other anomaly that continues to exist, and which this bill makes no effort to remove, has to do with expenditures by taxpayers on drugs. I am sure hon. members are well aware of the fact that the anomaly arises out of the difference in practice in relation to dispensing which is found in urban centres on the one hand, and rural areas on the other. In most cases it is the practice of the physician in the rural areas to dispense his own drugs and medicines. Consequently, the bill which the taxpayer receives from his physician includes the expenditure made on drugs and medicine, and those expenses are allowed by the Department of National Revenue as "extraordinary medical expenses." In the case of the urban dweller, he suffers what I feel is a discrimination. It is not the practice of physicians in urban areas to do their own dispensing. They simply issue a prescription which the patient or taxpayer takes to the dispensing druggist to be filled. The Department of National Revenue rejects expenditures made in that way for medicines and drugs.
Let us acknowledge, Mr. Speaker, that there are some administrative problems to be reckoned with in removing this anomaly and discrimination. I submit that these anomalies and discriminations should have been removed long ago, and I regret that no attempt is made in the present bill to remove them. I urge upon the Minister of Finance once more that between now and the next session of parliament he give further, and this time favourable, consideration to these matters.

Income Tax Act
to what are commonly known as profit sharing plans, and we are in effect here confirming what has been the practice with respect to those plans. Will the minister make a statement clarifying the relationship between this clause and assumed legal obligations? The matter was discussed at some length and arose out of decisions in the McCool case and the Rhinehorne case with reference to interest on assumed legal obligations.
The budget resolution seemed to indicate quite clearly that it was the intention of the ensuing legislation to place assumed legal obligations on precisely the same footing as those created directly by the taxpayer in the course of earning his income. I am not sure, however, even after carefully reading and rereading section 5, particularly the language of line 33, whether this does in fact include assumed legal obligations. If my understanding of the purpose of the section is correct, that it was intended to eliminate the decisions in the McCool and Rhinehorne cases and to place assumed legal obligations on precisely the same footing as primary obligations on the part of the taxpayer, then it remains a question whether the committee is satisfied that this language does actually carry out that intent. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

My own personal opinion would be that it does, that the language is sufficient to meet the point which my hon. friend has raised.

speechtext: Well, legal obligation refers to a legal obligation to pay interest. My hon. friend appreciates that. If the person who assumes the obligation assumes first an obligation to pay capital, and second an obligation to pay interest on it, I can assure him that the Department of National Revenue will interpret it in the way he suggests.

I have one question. Suppose a farmer buys a quarter-section of land which is covered with bush. He goes to work on this quarter-section. He borrows the money to clear off the bush. Can he deduct, for income tax purposes under this amendment, the interest on that borrowed money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is an interesting point that my hon. friend has made. As I have said before, I am always reluctant to give a legal opinion as to a specific case, but it seems to me to be the type of case that would qualify. My hon. friend has cited the case of a farmer who makes an investment in his farm and may have to borrow money either to clear it or to buy it. Under these circumstances he is entitled to deduct his expenses. It would seem to me, on the facts that the hon. member for Mackenzie has put, that he would be entitled to deduct the interest on the money he borrowed. I am not charging for that opinion, so do not hold me to it.

Let us take farmers who are clearing land west of the Calgary and Edmonton line in Alberta. In that area we have a lot of good land which is covered with bush. In order to work that farm a man gets the money somehow to clear the bush land so that it may be made productive. By "bush" I do not mean great trees, lumber containing trees, as they have them in British Columbia. At the present time he cannot charge off as an expense in his operation the money he has spent in clearing that land.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a capital expense.

That is regarded as a capital expense. I do not think that that is justified either. As a matter of fact, I do not know on what basis it is regarded as an expense, because in a practical way, as the hon. member well knows, there are large portions of the country which will prove productive if cleared. When I speak of bush I mean this scrub stuff that we have all over the place, and which is of no value. It gets

Income Tax Act
in your way; you have to burn it, and possibly that is the only thing you can do with it. I have never understood why that man is not permitted to charge something as an expense in clearing that farm so that it shall be valuable as a productive unit in agriculture. I do know that the present ruling is that he cannot charge one cent of that against his operations. That is something which deserves more consideration at the hands of those in authority. I put it down definitely so that if anybody wants to inquire I am referring at the moment to the district lying west of Cremona in my own constituency. I know that there we have that exact situation. I also know that at no place in the whole of the west, once it is cleared, is there a better place for growing coarse grains than on the very type of land that I am speaking about. I am not joking when I say that I know of lands which are growing a hundred bushels of oats to the acre. Surely it is that kind of production we want, because that happens to be a fairly wet area. I do think some consideration might be given to an alleviation of the situation of the man who has put in all his capital, and who gets no return for a couple of years in any event. Surely that should be considered.

I agree with the minister that in some cases the procedure of investing additional capital in clearing land was abused in the early days. I remember that in 1941 or 1942 it was allowed as a deduction, and there were a number of people in western Canada who, while not farmers, went out and invested a considerable amount of money in clearing lands, and then used it as a deduction.
As a result of that the department changed the regulation to provide that no deduction could be made for the clearing of land. Yet we know that in large areas of the west, including those referred to by the hon. member for Calgary West and the hon. member for Mackenzie, as well as in my own constituency, many young chaps have started out on their own on half-section farms. The money they have to reinvest each year to clear land should be deducted, so far as their income tax is concerned. I suggest some regulation should be made under which the half-section farmer at least will have this deduction. Perhaps it would be necessary to provide that those on larger farms, or those operating larger units, would not be permitted to make the deduction. As a matter of fact the large operator today with equipment of his own is allowed, I believe, $300 worth of clearing-often it is more than that-as a deduction. The small operator has not equipment of his own, but must go out

and hire it. Every cent he pays is from his capital, and he is not allowed a deduction on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The question whether money expended for the improvement of land should be a capital item or an operating cost item does not arise under this section. The hon. member for Mackenzie asked whether the interest on money borrowed for purposes of clearing land would be deductible. I said I thought it would be, because it would be a capital expenditure. The farmer would have borrowed it, and, as in respect of any other interest on capital investment, by way of mortgage or anything else, he would be entitled to deduct the interest. But the actual cost of improving the land has always been considered as a capital investment and not as a current operating expense.

One man has gone so far as to cut down the bush, break up the land and put it into condition so that he could get a crop off it. He did get a good crop, but in getting it he was not able to make a payment on his loan because he had to pay interest to the bank, and then pay income tax. The municipality had to wait another year because he had to pay income tax. In my view that is most unfair, because income tax is bound to be paid in respect of the wheat or grain taken off that land. Therefore why should he not be allowed, as a deduction from income tax, the expense of clearing the land?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That would meet with my convenience in relation to the discussion of the cases of persons receiving pensions out of a pension fund. However, I wish now to discuss another aspect of the matter, namely that relating to payments into a pension fund, which does come under this section.
The section we are amending states that the portion of trade union dues paid into a pension fund is allowed as an income tax deduction. I am not going to launch into an argument
Income Tax Act
about trade union dues generally, because the minister knows my thoughts on that matter. But may I point to certain facts, which I believe I can do most effectively by giving the details of a specific case.
The international typographical union has a pension plan. Under the laws of the union every active member thereof must pay dues that include a portion for pension purposes. Under the terms of this section of the act the income tax authorities have allowed that portion of the dues paid by members of the international typographical union which goes into the pension fund to be deducted for income tax purposes. I can speak from experience. I belong to this union and I get that small deduction at the end of the year.
It so happens that local No. 91, the Toronto local of the international typographical union, which has some 1,400 members in the greater Toronto area, has passed a local law which says that every member of the Toronto local must pay an additional one per cent in addition to the amount levied by head office. The plan has been approved by head office. So far as a member of the Toronto local is concerned, it is just as compulsory that he pay the extra one per cent as it is compulsory upon me as a member of the Winnipeg local to pay the basic pension assessment of two-and one-half per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As savings or as pension?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: As pension. If I die before I reach pensionable age it is gone. If I reach pensionable age it will come to me, unless I am still a member of this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Are there any unemployment benefits attached to the plan?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
No. The only other benefit attached to it is a mortuary benefit. If a person dies before he reaches pensionable age there is a mortuary benefit. The point I wish to make is that the extra one per cent I referred to is not voluntary. It is just as compulsory for a member of the Toronto local to pay the extra one per cent as it is for members of other branches of the union to pay the basic amount. Officials of the union have been in touch with the department in Ottawa to try to get them to agree to allow that extra amount. I have seen the correspondence, and I must say that I do not think the point has been recognized by the officials here. There has been some suggestion by officials here that one has to think of these plans in terms of amounts being deducted by the employer and paid into the fund. The act does not say that, and certainly it does not apply in the case of the basic amount we pay into our union pension fund.

Income Tax Act
That amount is not deducted by the employer. I pay it to the union and the union pays it into the pension fund. The same thing is done with regard to the extra one per cent at Toronto. In turn if a member of the Toronto union reaches pensionable age he will get an extra $5 a week in addition to the basic pension paid by the union which is now $16 a week. The extra $5 will be taxable income if the recipient is in a high enough bracket, but the one per cent that he is called upon to pay, in the same way that members of the other branches across Canada pay the basic amount, has not yet been allowed as an income tax deduction. It seems to me that the wording of the act is clear. I cannot see that there is any necessity for departmental approval of this; it should be automatic. I hope, despite the fact that the correspondence that has taken place thus far has not produced a favourable result, that such' will now be the case. I am sure the minister will agree with me on that, if I have stated the case correctly, and I am satisfied that I have. I have the correspondence, the laws of the international typographical union and the laws concerning the Toronto local plan before me. If there is any. doubt as to the wording of the act I suggest it should be changed to cover such a case. In the meantime I would be glad to have the minister's comment on it.

On section 7-Lease-option, hire-purchase, etc.

As I understand it, section 7 has the effect that in these lease-option agreements, or in fact agreements for sale, where the purchase price is to be paid over a period of years by instalments, the amounts of the annual payments will no longer be deductible as rent or an expense but will be included as a part of the purchase price and not deductible from income. I notice that no exception is made in the section, or so far as I can see any discretion given to the taxing authorities, to take account of what is almost a universal feature of such instalment payments, namely, that there is provision for interest on -the unpaid balance of the purchase price. In other words, if you sell under an agreement for sale at $5,000 to be paid at the rate of $1,000 a year, almost invariably there is a provision that interest at the rate of five per cent, let us say, will be payable on the unpaid balance together with the instalments of purchase price. I cannot see that anywhere in the section there is provision for that interest charge to be deducted from income. It is a genuine expense. It is not a part of the purchase price. It is merely interest on the unpaid balance, and I feel provision should be made for its deduction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I might say a word
in explanation of the amendment. Last year section 18, as contained in the act, applied to movable property. The essence of it was that if you agreed to rent machinery or equipment at $5,000 a year, and it was provided that at the end of five years-I am using that figure as an example-if you had paid the rent of $5,000 a year regularly the machinery would belong to you on payment of a further $100, that was looked upon as a capital expenditure. For purposes of depreciation the total rental payments would be aggregated together with the final payment on the option to purchase, and depreciation taken on that figure.
That only extended to movable property. As probably members of the committee are aware, it was found that this type of contract was being extended to real estate. In a good many cases, for instance, an insurance company will take over chain store properties at a figure. They will be leased by the store operator for so much a year, and the contract will provide that at the expiration of a certain period, upon payment of perhaps a fairly nominal sum, the so-called lessee will own the property. If that so-called lease extended over a reasonable period of time there would be no discrimination but if, as is sometimes the case, it was for a very short period, let us say for five years, and the depreciation which could be taken on -that type of property would

normally take twenty-five years to write down, then obviously the effect of such an arrangement would be to enable the so-called lessee to obtain accelerated depreciation at a rate which would not be available to the ordinary owner of a property.
It was felt that should be prevented. Mind you, I think I should say at once these arrangements are not entered into for the purpose of obtaining accelerated depreciation. They are entered into in order to enable the so-called lessee to improve his working capital position and not have too much money tied up in real estate. That is the purpose of the section. The general interest rule of course would apply with respect to moneys borrowed for legitimate purposes in connection with the business. That might cover the point raised by the hon. member for Kamloops.
Take a conditional sale agreement. Would it cover an ordinary conditional sale agreement of movable or immovable property? Would that come under the provisions of this amending section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that a conditional sale agreement would come under this section, and that the aggregate of the so-called rental and interest would be taken for the purpose of arriving at the capital cost against which depreciation could be taken as an expense.
I can see that, but what about the effect of the amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only effect of the amendment is to extend the operation of the clause to real property, that is, immovable property. Previously it only related to movables. Now it extends to immovable property, except that used by farmers.

Subsection 2 of the proposed
section 18 provides:
Where a person is deemed under subsection (1) to have acquired property under a contract or arrangement and the contract or arrangement is subsequently rescinded or determined, he shall, for the purpose of section 20, be deemed to have disposed of the property for the price fixed by the contract or arrangement minus the aggregate of all amounts paid by him under the contract or arrangement on account of the rent or other consideration.
From reading the section I take it he would then be penalized by having to pay tax on the amount of the payment already made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I am told that is not the case. He has been taking depreciation on the total sum, and this is to provide for the recapture principle in this type of contract.

It does not have the effect of penalizing him on the payment made, then?

I wanted to speak about this broad matter of the change we have made in our depreciation allowance. It will be remembered that when the minister spoke about it a year ago he was not too clear on just how it operated, but he did make the statement that it was a good thing for business. While far from being an expert, I have made some endeavour to understand this; and the opinions I have had from here and there are in pretty general agreement that this is a retrograde step in connection with depreciation. I realize that I should not say a thing like that without having some authority to support me, so I intend to read some short extracts from an article that appears in the February, 1950, issue of The Canadian Chartered Accountant. The heading is, "A long step backward. Diminishing balance depreciation." The writer is Kenneth F. Byrd, B.Sc. in economics, A.C.A., professor of accountancy at McGill university. He is a man who has had to look at these matters in various countries. On page 65 we find that he was born at Durban, South Africa, and his degrees and experience are given. He was dean of the faculty of commerce and administration at Natal university college, and was appointed professor of accountancy at McGill in 1947. He is a member of the Natal society of accountants and of the institute of chartered accountants in England and Wales. In this article this man, who obviously holds a very responsible position, does not pull any punches in what he has to say about what he calls this retrograde step we have taken. The article begins:
For many decades North America has been recognized as the home of the straight-line method of depreciation, and Britain, just as definitely, has been regarded as favouring the reducing instalment or diminishing balance method. Here, as in so many other fields of accounting practice, the division between the two countries has been clearly marked. It does not seem, however, to have been equally clearly noted that, five years ago, Britain came to the conclusion-
I am anxious that the minister should listen to this part.
-that her long clinging to the diminishing balance method was ill-advised and definitely harmful to the interests of good accounting.
He goes on as follows:
The Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales published on January 12, 1945, the ninth of its "Recommendations on Accounting Principles," dealing with the subject of depreciation. The recommendations included the statement that

the straight-line method "is used almost universally in the United States of America and Canada and to a large extent in this country. Though other methods may be appropriate in the case of some classes of assets the balance of informed opinion now favours the straight-line method as being the most suitable for general application." As regards the reducing balance method, "also largely used in this country," it warns that the percentage applied needs to be from two to three times that applied under the straight-line method. This is a fact not generally realized, the consequence being that rates of depreciation fixed on this basis may tend to be inadequate.
Then the author mentions our lapse, as he calls it. He says:
At last, therefore, it might be said that Britain and North America were of the same mind in regard to an important accounting method. Britain had come over to America's point of view. How definitely this was so may be seen in the following extract from a brilliant editorial on the subject, which appeared that time in The Accountant.
I need read only a short part of that editorial.
The outstanding point that will at once catch the attention of every reader is that the time-honoured reducing balance system is now so thoroughly deposed from its former popularity that it is not admitted even to be a second-rate alternative.
The rest of the quotation from The Accountant is interesting, but I go on to-quote the author again:
Scarcely, however, has this happy unanimity become a fact, outstanding among the other accounting principles and practices about which the two countries still disagree, when Canada decides that, for income tax purposes, the diminishing balance method is not such a bad idea after all. Her Minister of Finance, seeking ways of taking into account for income tax calculation the losses through obsolescence-
I do not have to read any further, but I go on to another portion of the article:
If, for income tax purposes, adoption of the diminishing balance method is the only means by which the income tax authorities can be induced to make any allowance for losses due to obsolescence, then, for these purposes only, the old, outdated method must be accepted. But surely this is not necessary. Normal obsolescence can be provided for by allowing a sufficiently generous annual depreciation rate on the straight-line basis, and it should be possible to allow for any abnormal loss at the time the asset is discarded.
The author then shows that South Africa did it by methods of that kind. Then, he comes back to the British experience. I am jumping a good deal of this, Mr. Chairman, but he says this:
Now, why, oh, why does one country not show more awareness of what has been learned by long and bitter experience in another? It is a very clearly established fact that Britain has proved, by decades of use, that the diminishing balance method is wholly unsatisfactory.
Yet, Mr. Chairman, that is the method which we, in the face of the experience in

other countries, are adopting in our country. I should like to read just two short extracts from the last of the article:
The serious thing about the proposed change for Canada is that it is a permanent shift from "straight-line" to "diminishing balance" depreciation.
The author goes on to call it a wolf in sheep's clothing, but I shall not bother about that. He concludes with this sentence:
The immediate danger is that Canada may, in an ill-advised moment, lose the benefits which she has thus far gained from her long adherence to straightline depreciation. Let her give heed to the experience of those who have learned that the "lazy accountant's friend"-
That is the name given to this method.
-that the "lazy accountant's friend" is a wolf in sheep's clothing.
As I indicated at the beginning, I have not sufficient knowledge of this matter to discuss it intelligently, but I have brought as a witness a man who I think is outstanding, and who completely condemns the retrograde step we took last year. I have one other question to ask, and then I am going to sit down. I have not yet heard, it may be through my inattention, any reason why farmers and fishermen should have been granted the option of using the straight-line method or the diminishing balance method. I think it was covered by the Minister of National Revenue the last time the subject was discussed in the house, but speaking from memory, I have not heard why, in this instance, farmers and fishermen should be treated any differently from the man who has a little machine shop in the same town, where the farmer comes to get his work done.
Then I believe the farmer or fisherman had to make his choice within a given time. I suppose that time has now expired or is near expiration. I should like to hear from the minister, first as to what he thinks about this step we have taken, the retrograde step as I call it, or the long step backwards as this author calls it. I should like to hear about that, and then I should like to hear him answer this question. If it was a fair thing for the fishermen and the farmers, why was it not a fair thing to the small businessman?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I read the article by Professor Byrd in the magazine to which my hon. friend referred. He is a professor of accountancy at my own university, and consequently, if for no other reason, a highly competent member of the staff. I am sure it represents his considered and genuine opinion as to the diminishing balance method of depreciation as against the straight-line method, but I am sure that Professor Byrd would be the first to recognize that there
Income Tax Act
can be other opinions on this point. We would not assert for a moment that his opinion was necessarily conclusive. I can tell my hon. friend that there are a great many other persons, in whose judgment and technical capacity I have equal confidence, who have expressed exactly the opposite opinion to me. I may say that includes the chartered accountants association. As I say, it is a matter of opinion, and I am not going to attempt to impose my own opinion on the committee. I came to the conclusion that the provision set out last year was the preferable method in Canada, and the house adopted it. It is now law.
As to the reason why farmers and fishermen were exempted from the operation of the new principle, if the hon. member was in the house he will recall that almost all the farmer members rose and said that this was a terrible thing for the farmers; that they did not keep their books in such a way, or most of them did not keep their books in such a way, that they could readily calculate from year to year on this diminishing balance principle. Being a good-natured sort of a fellow, I did not want to impose on them something which seemed to be objectionable, so I excluded them from the operation of the act. I did make a statement at the time that I thought after they had studied it some of them might feel the diminishing balance principle might be advantageous. I just expressed that opinion. This year some of them seem to have changed their mind. Evidently some of them think that I was right because I have had representations since to the effect that they ought to be allowed to use this new method. So again, being good natured and always willing to listen to suggestions of this kind, I have put in a provision for that. The committee will see there is a provision in here which makes it optional. Once having exercised the option, of course you must stay with it. You cannot switch back and forth from one kind of depreciation to the other; but the option is there. Any small farmer who may find it difficult to keep records in such a way that he can operate on this principle, which apparently requires the keeping of slightly more detailed records, can continue on the straight-line basis. That was the reason for making the exception for farmers and fishermen.

May I follow up with some supplementary questions? I want to find out how far the minister will go with me. Do you agree with the professor that it has been in vogue in England for a

Income Tax Act
great many years and has now been discarded, and that it is not used in the United States? In fact, Canada is now the only place using it that I know of. Would that be right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that that is not correct. They may have partially discontinued it in England. I cannot speak for certain as to that. That however does not prove anything.

If the professor says that-this man who guides your children and your children's children in your universities, and having the reputation you gave him -we, would not suspect him of telling us an absolute untruth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. But of course he might be mistaken.

The minister says he may toe mistaken. He quotes the accountant in England in the article which he quoted from, where they say identically the same thing that he says. We may be bright enough to rake over some old bones and find some phosphorus or sulphur in them, if we work hard enough. But after all, is it not a fact-whether we are right or wrong; leave that out of the consideration-that we have launched out all by ourselves on something which other -countries have discarded?

The usual method of computing annual wear and tear is what is termed the reducing balance method. In other words in ascertaining the wear and tear for any year the agreed percentage is calculated on original cost progressively reduced by . each allowance. In some cases, particularly ships and commercial aircraft, the straight-line method is adopted, that is the annual allowance is calculated at a percentage of the original cost. This latter method can now, by arrangement with the inland revenue, in accordance with the terms of the Finance Act 1949, be extended to any machinery or plant, but the percentages are subject to negotiation.
So that in the United Kingdom all machinery and plant can now be placed on the straight-line depreciation basis, although formerly the diminishing balance applied to all that type of equipment. With respect to new farm buildings we find the following: '

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

It has suffered no capital depreciation, because the only justification enabling a taxpayer to take depreciation from current income is on the assumption that in fact the value of his property has gone down; but if on the contrary it has gone up, he is not entitled to depreciation. The building would unquestionably be ten years older, and the bricks may have a slightly more mellow colour, but if he is able to sell it for $10,000 it is quite clear

that he has not taken any capital loss, and the depreciation which a man charges to income for depreciable assets is in fact a capital charge, and it is intended to reimburse him for his capital outlay. If in fact he has not lost any capital then he should not have charged it to income, and that is the basis of the recapture principle.

That seems to me to do what in fact this other article to which reference has been made said the department was doing, namely, setting up an entirely new basis for depreciation, not merely changing the method of calculating depreciation, but changing it from the straight line basis, to a diminishing balance basis, but in fact setting up a totally new concept of depreciation. Is not that so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, I concede to my hon. friend that it is undoubtedly a very complicated subject; but whether it is straight line depreciation, or whether it is on the diminishing balances principle, what you are doing is amortizing the capital cost. That is the fundamental principle of depreciation. The only difference in the act now is a difference in method, and the difference in method is that instead of a straight line method of applying five per cent, ten per cent or fifteen per cent, or whatever it is, over the period of years in which depreciation is exhausted, you start off with the same capital cost. You depreciate at a higher figure in the early years, and then you work down until it arrives, theoretically, at nothing. Of course, if you are on a percentage basis you get down to a fraction of a dollar; but, in effect, it will be nothing.
However, there is no difference in the principle of taking depreciation under either system. It is a process of amortization of a capital expenditure, a recognition of the principle that you should not pay tax on something which is going to disappear. That underlies the whole basis of depreciation.
On the other point I readily recognize that the provisions of this section are extremely complicated and extremely difficult for the average layman to understand, and even for the lawyer to understand. As I said at the outset of my remarks, one reason why they have to be lies in the fact that we have eliminated discretions here. Of course it would be very simple to make a short and easily understood section by saying, "in such amount as the minister may determine,"-and that was the system we used to have.
This amendment is a relieving measure. If you purchase additional assets of the same class you can group them and, instead of having to pay tax on the excess portion of depreciation which, in fact, has not been

needed, you are getting accelerated depreciation on your new assets. And the second group, group B, covers the case where there has been less.
It is long and complicated but, in defence of the draftsmen, chief of whom was the assistant deputy minister of justice, for whom I have high regard as a draftsman, I do think that it fully and clearly and accurately sets out the contingencies which have to be met. I cannot say anything further about the drafting.
I freely confess I had to study it pretty carefully before I realized how it operated; but I did finally come to the conclusion that it would cover the case to which I have been referring. What does the minister say in answer to the specific question raised by those who disagree with this method, that it distorts altogether the actual rate of depreciation, making it much too high in the earlier years and too low in the later years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In my view it comes much closer to the actual facts. Take the case of the ordinary motorcar. Everyone knows that in the initial year the car depreciates more than it does on the straight line basis. It depreciates up to 30 per cent right away. That is why I believe-and I may believe it wrongly-that the diminishing plan principle, where you have a higher percentage in the earlier years, is a fair principle.

The minister has picked out one particular category to illustrate his proposition, and his illustration is not sound. For instance, let us consider industrial plant machinery, where it is generally agreed that new equipment and machinery installed in a plant in fact does not reach maximum output and a level of peak efficiency for perhaps two years after the machinery has been brought into use; whereas, under this reducing plan method the depreciation in the first year is very great, and in the second, third and fourth years it is considerably less. The fact is that the machinery is more valuable to the industry after the second year's operations, when the kinks have been ironed out, and the new product has found its market.
It seems to me that there is a good case, an almost unanswerable case, for those who-say that if you take a straight line method of depreciation it will give you a picture-while not exactly parallel, nevertheless much.

I will make one final comment. What the minister has said seems to me to prove that here we have a case where a few particular circumstances will be suited by this method, but that it will be unsuitable to the great majority of cases. It is true that under special circumstances it was thought necessary to give accelerated depreciation, but that was a special procedure worked out to fit special cases in wartime. In the same way that accelerated depreciation is not necessary in the normal run of cases I submit that the diminishing balance method is not suitable now. I say this is a wrong principle which will fit only a few special cases, but that the straight-line method is still of much more general application throughout the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

On section 19-Evasion of tax.

I should like to suggest to the minister that the word "wilfully" be changed to "fraudulently". As I understand the state of the law, tax evasion is not necessarily illegal. If a man has been able to take advantage of a tax concession granted by law, then it may be an evasion but not an illegal evasion. For instance, if a taxpayer owns a company which does not enjoy the tax concession in respect to its first $10,000 of earnings and sells part of his shareholdings to bring himself within the tax concession, that is legal. I do not see how any tax can be evaded unless it is wilful, in the sense of being intentional. It has to be intentional.	But it is not therefore
necessarily wrong or illegal. I do not think the word wilful is a word that has been clearly determined in law, but I think "fraudulent" has. No one objects to the intent of the clause under consideration, but I think a real intent to evade the tax must be proven, and the wording should so indicate. I would suggest tha-t "fraudulently evaded" is the phrase that should be used. In law "fraudulent" has long had a clear and well known interpretation. In a section of such serious import I question the advisability therefore of using new words which might be interpreted in a way that would not agree with what I believe the minister intends, namely, that the section should deal with fraudulent evasion of tax payments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for his suggestion. I asked about this myself, and the Department of Justice used this language. They asserted that it should be done because the word "wilful" is the word used in section 120, subsection (3), which reads:
Where a person has been convicted under this section of wilfully, in any manner, evading or attempting to evade, payment of taxes imposed by part I, he is net liable to pay a penalty imposed...

I hope the minister will

Income Tax Act

Is not the governing word actually "evade"?

No.
That is a dangerous word.
This word "wilfully" has to be decided by the courts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

On section 21-Certain organizations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is a section which I am sure will oe of interest to all hon. members. Before we discuss it perhaps I might say just a word about it. There is an amendment to be made, but before I indicate what that amendment is I would point out the-

Income Tax Act
general purpose of the section. The present section in the act which exempts from tax the income of certain charitable organizations -and it is section 57 which exempts from tax various types of organizations-reads as follows:
(e) an organization operated exclusively for charitable purposes or an agricultural organization, a board of trade or a chamber of commerce, no part of the income of which was payable to, or was otherwise available for the personal benefit of, any proprietor, member or shareholder thereof.
The committee will appreciate the fact that over the years there have been built up various types of charitable organizations including those known as the so-called charitable foundations-the Massey foundation, the Canadian foundation and so on-where capital gifts are made to the foundation, where sometimes income is paid in and where the moneys appropriated are used for charitable objectives, given to hospitals and the like to be expended. In the past it is questionable whether those organizations have been clearly entitled to the exemption. I am sorry to say that in addition there has been an opportunity for abuse in the case of these charitable foundations; that is to say, moneys could be accumulated in them and not actually paid over to charities. Then the charitable foundation could be wound up and the owners or proprietors get the money back, although in the meantime tax exemption privileges would have been obtained. It was felt both necassary and desirable to plug that loophole. Let me hasten to say that this does not apply by any means to the really bona fide, genuine charitable foundation. Without going into detail, one particular case was drawn to our attention which made me feel that an amendment to the act was called for.

Was that case in the province
of Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, it was a case in the province of Quebec, actually; in my own province. The section now provides for dividing these charitable foundations or organizations into two groups. One is:
(ea) a charitable organization, whether or not incorporated, all the resources of which were devoted to charitable activities carried on by the organization itself and no part of the income of which was payable to, or was otherwise available for the personal benefit of, any proprietor, member or shareholder thereof.
Then there is the (eb) section which covers the so-called charitable foundation. On examining the section the committee will notice that there are laid down certain conditions which would permit this type of corporation to qualify as a charitable foundation and to obtain the exemption from income tax which would flow from that quality. As the

sections appear in the bill, there is a clear line of demarcation between the charitable organization which carries on charitable activities itself and the foundation which turns over all its assets or 90 per cent of its receipts to charitable objectives. In the first case under the defining section which we passed earlier, the donor to the organization could claim an exemption within the 5 per cent limit in the case of a corporation and the 10 per cent limit in the case of individuals for gifts made to the charitable organization. But as drafted, the charitable foundation would not qualify such a donor for exemption. It was pointed out to us that there were some cases in which these groups performed both these functions. They not only conducted charitable activities themselves but they also turned over moneys out of their revenues to charitable objectives like hospitals, universities or whatever it may be. We therefore studied whether it would not be possible, while retaining the protective provisions to which I have referred, to give this second class of charitable organization a similar quality which would enable people who made gifts of income to that so-called charitable foundation to deduct this for income tax purposes. The effect of the amendment which I am going to move is this. Perhaps I had better read the amendment. It is as follows:
There shall be included in computing a corporation's income all gifts received by the corporation other than gifts received subject to a trust or direction that the property given, or property substituted therefor, is to be held by the corporation for the purpose of gaining or producing income therefrom.
In other words, the onus will be put upon the donor to say when he gives to the charitable foundation that his gift is a gift of income or of capital; but from the point of view of the tax department, all receipts by the foundation will be considered as income unless the foundation shows that they have been paid over on the advice that they are a gift of capital and that the capital is to be invested and the income only used for charitable purposes. That explanation may not be as clear as it should be, but I have tried to summarize the provisions of the section. I will welcome any discussion by members of the committee.
In the first place, do I understand that this provision applies to charitable foundations in existence at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From June 1, 1950. The section so provides.
Only those coming into existence on or after June 1, 1950. Is that what the minister means?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
I am referring to the date of the creation of the charitable foundation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The charitable foundation can be created before or after; but the particular requirements with respect to the distribution of 90 per cent of its income and so on apply as and from June 1, 1950.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would apply to the 1950 taxation year.

I think that is quite clear, but I wanted the minister's confirmation of it. It is quite clear then that this provision may deprive some charitable foundations of an exemption which they hitherto enjoyed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. I do not think it is going to deprive them of anything.
I am sorry, but I do not read the amendment in the same way as the minister does.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Perhaps it would be better to have the amendment read before we debate it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That clause 21 be amended by renumbering subclause (3) as subclause (4) and Inserting the following immediately after subclause (2) :
(3) The said section fifty-seven is further amended by adding the following subsection thereto:
"(3) For the purpose of paragraph (eb) of subsection (1)
(a)	a corporation shall be deemed not to have acquired control of another corporation if it has not purchased (or otherwise acquired for a consideration) any of the shares in the capital stock of that corporation, and
(b)	there shall be included in computing a corporation's income all gifts received by the corporation other than gifts received subject to a trust or direction that the property given, or property substituted therefor, is to be held by the corporation for the purpose of gaining or producing income therefrom."

My observations, Mr. Chairman, are not affected particularly by the amendment. I should like some information as to the extent to which section 21 of the bill applies. I think the minister's answer has made it quite clear that this amendment -whatever the effect of it might be-does apply to all so-called charitable foundations in existence. It does not apply only to those that may come into existence after the date of the enactment of this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite right.

Therefore if there is anything to be said for or against retroactivity as applied to legislation affecting charitable foundations, then those who object to application of such legislation to charitable foundations in existence had better speak now or forever hereafter hold their peace.
Income Tax Act
The other point on which I should like to have some confirmation from the minister is this. I take it that the underlying purpose of the proposed amendment is to compel charitable foundations, so called, to disburse the income that they receive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they want to claim the taxation exemption.
Quite. If they wish to enjoy the benefit of exemption from income tax then they must disburse their income as they go along to the extent of 90 per cent of that income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

Back of that must be the view that it is unhealthy to permit charitable foundations to set up businesses and to claim immunity from taxing statutes, and simply to accumulate funds or accumulate control of corporations or businesses. I may say, sir, that with that intent I am in fuil accord, and I hope that this committee of the whole will be in complete accord with it.
I would have been interested to hear from the hon. member for Leeds, had he been in the house, and perhaps any other hon. members who may have spoken against similar Ontario legislation on the hustings in the byelection campaign several months ago in the Ontario constituency of Leeds.

I should like to ask the minister one question on paragraph (eb), subparagraph (i) which reads:
Did not carry on any business.
^ If a charitable organization is established, the creature of a revenue-producing business already in existence, it cannot now carry on any commercial activities. Is that the intent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. It is quite possible that some of these charitable foundations which have been created prior to this time may in fact control certain businesses through stock ownership. This does not interfere with that at all. There is no retroactivity effect to this legislation. They may have accumulated their income right up to this time and not paid a bit of it out, but in future in order to continue to qualify they must pay out 90 per cent of their current income. We are not interfering with any practices that may have been followed in the past, but in future they must qualify, and in future it will not be possible for any charitable foundation to acquire control by purchase of shares of a business.

Can the minister give us an estimate of the revenue that the government has lost on account of these so-called charitable foundations that have been established in Canada?

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is almost impossible to ascertain. I do not want it understood for a moment that I think there has been any widespread abuse of the possibilities which perhaps the charitable foundations would afford in the hands of someone who wanted to use it for that purpose. But the rules which we are setting up here seem to provide a fairly good test for the bona fide charitable institution, which I think is very desirable. I do not want to discourage them for a moment, but I think certain safeguards are needed in order to see that the provisions are not abused. I want to reiterate, that there is no retroactive effect to this whatever.

The purpose of my question was to find out whether the government has any knowledge as to the extent of loss of revenue to the country, on account of the establishment of charitable foundations. That is something the house should know about, because the more of these we get and the more they multiply the more burden is placed upon the remainder of the taxpayers of the country. That is the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The point of course is there is no burden so long as 90 per cent of the revenues of these foundations is paid out for genuinely charitable -purposes. The donations to them can only be made out of income to the extent of the 10 per cent or 5 per cent limits, and gifts of course would be exempt from gift tax; but with these reservations- we have given this a good deal of thought- the protective measures which we are putting in here are adequate; but at the same time I think they are fair.

Then a revenue-producing corporation must disperse 90 per cent of its revenue? Assume it is a profit-producing corporation. I can think of a number; I can think of some of the drug trusts in the United States. In that country some universities have the right to manufacture certain drugs that one of their professors has discovered. I think the university of Wisconsin is one of them. There may be cases like that in Canada where there are revenue-producing corporations. Under this act the corporation to be classed as a charitable organization must distribute 90 per cent of its profits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not the way my hon. friend put it. We must be careful not to confuse the situation in the United States with the situation in Canada. In the United States they have a law whereby the taxability of a corporation depends upon the quality of the person who owns it. I am told that Columbia university is operating spaghetti factories, and all kinds of industrial corporations, and

these industrial corporations are exempt from the ordinary corporation taxes because they are owned by Columbia university. I hope that we shall never have that principle in Canada. But let us take the case of -a charitable foundation that owns 5 per cent of the shares of a profitable spaghetti company.
Or a newspaper?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Or a newspaper, or anything else you like. The newspaper is not obliged 'to distribute in dividends any more than the board of directors feels is- proper; but all dividends received by the charitable foundation which owns the shares of the spaghetti factory, or the newspaper or anything else, must be distributed for charitable purposes to the extent of 90 per cent in the year received. It does not affect the commercial company which is operating a profitable business, because under this section a corporation to qualify as a charitable foundation must be one in which no part of the income was payable to or otherwise available for the personal benefit of any proprietor, member or shareholder thereof. I think the section is pretty tight.
The minister brought out the Columbia university. That was the case I was trying to dig out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is owing to the difference in the law.
I hope we never get to that stage in Canada. I agree with the minister on that. A corporation may then continue to make a profit so long as it does not pay it over to the charitable foundation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is to be hoped the corporation would continue to make profit as long as possible. That is what it is in business for. The dividend policy of the corporation will be determined by its board of directors, but as I say if a profitable corporation is controlled by a charitable foundation the earnings of the corporation as available in dividends to the charitable foundation can now be distributed to a charitable foundation.
I understand that if a charitable trust is carrying on any business, it would be disqualified under this section; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not say it would be disqualified under the section. It would be disqualified only if any of the profits of the business it was carrying on inured to the personal benefit of any proprietor, member or shareholder. If it is a charitable foundation it cannot carry on commercial business. It could do it of course through a corporation, if it had the shares of a corporation in a

fashion other than by purchase, or if they had been acquired before the coming into force of this act.
Section stands.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I have the consent of the house to revert to motions for the purpose of communicating to the house a statement about which the leader of the opposition inquired when the orders of the day were called earlier this afternoon?
I would like to read to the house the full text of an announcement made in London today, with which our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) was associated. The following statement was issued today (Thursday) in London:
During their talks last week, the foreign ministers of France, the United Kingdom and the United States considered how the countries of western Europe and North America might improve their co-operation on economic problems which require adjustments by them in the period immediately ahead. The emphasis in their discussions was on the positive courses of action which need to be taken.
The Secretary of State of the United States emphasized the great value of the existing relationship between the organization for European economic co-operation and the United States and believed that it would be helpful to broaden this relationship to provide for regular discussion and consideration of the problems requiring co-operative action in the coming period. He pointed out that, while the European recovery program terminates in 1952, the interest of the United States in Europe will necessarily continue and that study of the problems is now going forward actively in the United States on the highest governmental level. During conversations this week, the Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs has indicated a similar interest on the part of his country to participate in the study of these problems. The four ministers believe that this relationship would permit a close co-ordination of the work now going forward in the United States and Canada on these problems with the parallel efforts of the OEEC.
The foreign ministers of France and the United Kingdom, after consultation with the chairman of the OEEC, stated their hope that the OEEC would invite Canada and the United States to establish, on an informal basis, a working relationship with the OEEC whereby the two countries could join with the OEEC in the discussion and consideration of the action to be taken on these problems.
It was agreed that the proposed working relationship between Canada, the United States, and the OEEC would not interfere with the present functions of the OEEC as an organization devoted primarily to European economic problems as provided in the convention for European economic cooperation.
The four ministers were in agreement that the economic and financial problems arising from the
55946-166J
North Atlantic Treaty
defence effort fell primarily within the competence of the North Atlantic treaty organization. They recognized also the concern of the North Atlantic treaty with broader questions of economic relations among the signatory countries and welcomed the decision of the council to have the deputies consider what further action should be taken under article 2 of the treaty.
The four ministers were further agreed that it was their hope, through a new working relationship, to proceed promptly toward finding solutions of the general economic problems which lie immediately ahead along lines which would eliminate conflict in their international economic policie's. They recognize that Canada, the United States and the western European countries have a continuing interest in developing and strengthening economic collaboration between them in order that they can make together their full contribution to the building of a peaceful and prosperous world order. They further recognize that the development and strengthening of the economic ties of this community of nations may in the future require formal organizational expression, but they believe it is unnecessary at this time to attempt to suggest precisely what form of arrangement will prove to be best suited to assist the taking of common action by the community.
The Canadian government welcomes this statement. If the organization for European economic co-operation invites us to establish an informal working relationship with them we shall be glad to accept.
It may be helpful to members of the house if I say a few words about the OEEC. This organization was set up after General Marshall's famous speech of June 5, 1947. In that speech he called on the European countries to draw together. Sixteen countries* including the United Kingdom and Ireland and almost all the continental countries free from Russian domination, responded. As their organization developed, much of its work related to Marshall aid; the members considered together their needs for special * assistance and presented programs and reports to the economic co-operation administration, headed by Mr. Paul Hoffman, in Washington. But the OEEC was never intended merely as a channel to facilitate the provision of Marshall aid. Its purposes were wider and longer than that. It was designed, as its name indicates, to promote co-operation among European countries in all matters of common economic interest and on a permanent basis. It has already reduced many of the trade restrictions between European countries. It has fostered trade by means of currency arrangements designed to make strict bilateral balance and barter unnecessary as between members. In these and other ways it is strengthening Europe economically and therefore politically.
This, then, is the organization with which we may be invited to associate. The European organization might thus be extended to estab-ish an informal relationship with Canada and

North Atlantic Treaty the United States in the discussion and consideration of economic problems of common interest. Thus it may become an organization for North American-Western European cooperation.
I am sure the house will be pleased to know that at the same time as such arrangements for informal economic co-operation in the immediate future are going forward the deputies to the North Atlantic council are to consider further the question of longer-term collaboration under article 2 of the treaty.
In conclusion I should perhaps stress that our new association would be informal. It would involve a recognition that the economic problems faced by OEEC countries, the United States and ourselves are common problems, not isolated individual problems. In the last analysis solutions must depend on action by individual countries, but they should be sought and discussed jointly around a common table.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TEXT OF ANNOUNCEMENT MADE IN LONDON THIS DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate myself and, in doing so, I am sure all members of the party to which I belong, with the expression of approval of every forward step which will bring together in closer and more effective co-operation the nations of the European community on the Atlantic and in North America. What has been given to us now as the official statement coming from the meeting in London does not report conclusions of such a broad nature as had been suggested in the press. I merely mention that because there was certain speculation earlier about something of a more positive nature. Nevertheless I feel there will be great encouragement in the fact that the . very presentation of this statement indicates that the nations of the Atlantic community are extending their consideration beyond the military aspects of the North Atlantic charter, and are recognizing the necessity of implementing the general provisions of article 2 as complementary to the purposes of article 1.
Undoubtedly economic and military strength go hand in hand. Without economic strength and economic co-operation the military strength upon which our hopes of peace depend could not possibly be maintained as a reality. If through military co-operation based upon economic co-operation the stability and peace which we all desire result, then it will be possible to carry this [DOT] association still further to the fulfilment of the purpose of article 2 and to the strengthening of those very institutions, and the understanding thereof which is in itself an essential part of the whole purpose of the treaty. While the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has made it clear that what is contemplated at present

is simply an informal arrangement, nevertheless I hope there will be a sufficient measure of formality and of clarity of defined association to give us hope that the termination of these discussions, with continuing and effective association for military purposes, will be carried into the economic and social sphere as well, that this may in truth be the beginning of a far closer collaboration of the nations of the Atlantic community, and that we may in fact be seeing the beginning of a really workable world association for peace and stability in the years ahead.

subtopic: TEXT OF ANNOUNCEMENT MADE IN LONDON THIS DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I noted that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) stated that he was speaking for his party as well as for himself. May I say we are pleased to associate ourselves with the remarks he has made. We have always emphasized the importance of article 2 of the Atlantic agreement. I am very glad indeed to learn that the conference has come to some informal arrangement regarding the implementation of that part of the agreement. I believe that economic understanding among the north Atlantic nations is at least as important as military arrangements. If we can bring about reasonable and decent economic conditions among the nations of the world I feel that in time we shall manage, as the leader of the opposition said in his closing remarks, to eliminate the prospect of future war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Here is the position. It was felt that a good many of these appeals could

be heard by one member of the board.
