On section 32-Private company election.

Here we are back on this group of sections again. I think this is the third time I have started to offer a suggestion to the minister in the hope of simplifying and clarifying these very difficult sections. I am suggesting that the minister take this in five stages. The first would be to trace through this new legislation the position of the individual shareholder, that is, the non-corporate shareholder; second, the position of the corporate minority shareholder under these

Income Tax Act
sections and in relation to section 27 of the act; third, the position of the corporate controlling shareholder before May 10; fourth, the position of the corporate controlling shareholder after May 10; fifth, the position of the corporate controlling shareholder in reference to subsidiaries of subsidiaries.
Mr. Chairman, those are suggestions to the minister. I think if the minister can clarify the position, or the effect of those amendments at those five stages, he will have helped the committee to understand these provisions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend appreciates that these sections apply only to private companies as defined in the terms of the section, and that was the principle that was applied to similar measures following the recommendation of the Ives commission. Take the case which he puts up first, of the individual shareholder of a private corporation which has accumulated a surplus.
This is a corporation with less than seventy-five shareholders?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
According to the definition of the act, that is right. A corporation may elect to pay fifteen per cent tax on that accumulated surplus, which thereupon becomes capitalized and then becomes a tax-paid surplus. It may not pay on any part of it; it must pay a tax on the whole thing, so far as the arrears are concerned. Now, when that has been done, it becomes a tax-paid capital surplus. The corporation may capitalize it, and it then becomes a capital surplus which can be distributed in accordance with the law governing corporations in so far as the distribution of capital is concerned. It could take the form of a stock dividend; it could take the form of a distribution for the reduction of capital. My hon. friend is a lawyer, and he will appreciate that when one is effecting a distribution of capital under the company law relating to the particular company, whatever the requirements of the particular company law for the reduction of capital are must be observed; that is the case of an individual shareholder.
In the case of a corporate minority shareholder, he would be in exactly the same position as an individual shareholder. The corporation would have capitalized this undistributed surplus, and it could then be capitalized and distributed to corporate minority shareholders and would not be taxable in the hands of that shareholder.
Will that be so after we have adopted section 11 of the bill which amends section 27 of the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; section 11 will not interfere with that situation. Section 11 only

applies to the future acquisition of control, so the ordinary rules apply, and the dividends from corporation to corporation are free as between one Canadian taxpayer and another where control was previously acquired.
I think I have answered the third question as a result of my hon. friend's interjection.
I think I have answered both three and four. I have dealt with both prior to, and subsequent to, May 10. The fifth question concerns the position of the corporate controlling shareholder of a subsidiary of a subsidiary. I must confess that I get a little lost there. I think the same rules apply though, no matter how far you carry it through. What is referred to in the section as a designated surplus, that is the surplus any particular company has which exists on May 10, can be dealt with in the way I have indicated; that is, it could be capitalized upon the payment of the fifteen per cent tax, and the earnings subsequent to May 10 will follow the ordinary rule and can be paid to another company tax free as between those companies, if the other company is a Canadian tax paying company; or the matching principle can be applied on future dividends when earned, and an individual corporation may capitalize, upon payment of the fifteen per cent tax, an amount equivalent to the part which it pays out in cash dividends.
And that can be carried right through, one degree after another, from subsidiary to subsidiary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I am right on that. I confess I have not given any thought to that particular condition. I see no reason why it should not be so.
Did the minister say that the privilege of paying the fifteen per cent had to be exercised in respect of the whole amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right, all the existing surplus up to the end of 1949.
Where does the minister find that in the legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is in section 95A (1) which reads as follows:
A private company may elect, in prescribed manner and in prescribed form, to be assessed and to pay a tax of fifteen per cent on an amount equal to its undistributed income on hand at the end of the 1949 taxation year minus its tax paid undistributed income as of that time.
Then subsection (2) covers the accumulation of earnings for the future, or what I refer to as the matching principle.
Has not the minister amended that?

I want to go back to the provisions of section 11 of the bill, to be sure I understand that the provisions of subsection 1 are applicable where the receiving corporation acquired control of the payer corporation after May 4, which is now May 10.
I am not clear on how far that limitation goes. It seems to me that is going to cut out two classes of cases, and the reason for cutting them out I do not see. One is when a company acquiring the shares already controls, through ownership of shares, another company, the company whose shares are transferred; second, a case where a company acquired shares, and the company whose shares are acquired is controlled directly or indirectly by the same company. The narrow wording that is used in section 11 seems to exclude that and yet I cannot see why, in principle, those cases should be excluded.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not quite clear that I see what my hon. friend's difficulty is. The purpose of section 11 is to put a cut-off date with respect to the acquisition of control and provide that those surpluses can only be disposed of by capitalizing them under the provisions of section 95A so far as arrears are concerned. So far as the future is concerned, in disposing of their earnings, they may accumulate to the extent that they distribute in cash; and that applies whether it is a company which is now controlling a company which has a large accumulated surplus, or which acquires control in the future. My remarks relate entirely to private companies. The committee will appreciate that we are not talking about public companies at all.
I am coming to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When we say "private companies", those are the relatively closely held companies.

I still come back to the wording of subsection 2 of section 11, which seems to say that the provisions of subsection 1 are applicable where the receiving corporation acquired control of the payer corporation after May 10. That is really what is meant, that it only becomes effective where that receiver corporation acquired control of a payer corporation after May 10?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; we are not interfering with arrangements that have been made prior to May 10.
Why does it only apply to private companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The answer to that is this. This method of providing a means whereby accumulated surpluses of closely held companies
Income Tax Act
could be distributed without too great penalty arose following the investigations made by the Ives commission. Part XVIII of the old act provided that surpluses of private companies could be capitalized and distributed upon payment of a tax which was something of the order of 20 per cent. We decided to extend that provision to companies which had accumulated surpluses beyond that time. It is a new move. One might say that in logic there is no reason why it should not be applied to public companies; but the Ives commission report did not recommend that it should be. We thought that for the time being we would proceed fairly slowly here and make it apply to the same class of companies that were dealt with under part XVIII of the old act. After we have seen how this works for a year, it may be possible to extend it to public companies. But this sort of legislation could have quite significant effects on the market quotations of publicly held companies, and I really did not feel that I wanted to go that far in this initial step. I am proceeding a bit cautiously here. Frankly, that is the reason why we have restricted it to the same class of company to which the old part XVIII applied.

There is a question I should like to raise, and I should like to get clarification-although I think I know what the answer is-for the sake of the record. Under this bill there is no intention to deal in any way with a public company which has shares listed on the stock exchange and which may have a large surplus. There is no intention under this act to force that surplus into dividends or distribution or to force a public company to distribute its surplus. I ask that question, although I think I know the answer, in order to get the situation adequately cleared up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. Neither is there the intention of doing so nor does the proposed legislation do so. It does not affect public companies. It relates only to private companies as defined.

I wish to say that I think the use of the term "private company" is unfortunate. If the legislation had retained the expression used by the minister in his budget speech, namely, "closely held corporation," I think it would be much better. When we came to the budget resolution we found this expression "private company" instead of the earlier and better expression "closely held corporation".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry, but I was consulting my officials and did not catch that.

I just said that I regretted that when the budget resolution was introduced it used the expression "private company" rather than the clearer expression "closely

Income Tax Act
held corporation" which the minister used in his budget speech. The expression "private company", of course, under the Companies Act has a definite statutory significance. In this bill this expression "private company" has no relation whatsoever to "private company" as that expression is used in the Companies Act. In other words, the kind of company that is contemplated here may be either a private or a non-private company, provided it has not more than 75 shareholders on its share record. In order to avoid confusion on the part of people reading this legislation hereafter, will the minister not consider dropping this expression "private company"? I am sure many people who will read this legislation are going to treat it as the equivalent of the expression "private company" as used in the Companies Act, and that will be misleading. Will the minister not give consideration to using that earlier expression "closely 'held corporation"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be glad to give consideration to it. But may I say that the reason we used it was that in part XVIII, which has been in the law for some time, the phrase "private company" was used, and we have been using it here again. I think in the trade it has come to be fairly well known among lawyers and accountants who are advising with respect to these things. I think it is fairly clearly known what it was, and that is why I retained it. The phrase "closely held corporation" is an excellent colloquial expression, but I do not know that it is much more accurate than "private company". I realize my hon. friend's point that "private company" under the Companies Act has a certain specific meaning with certain conditions attached to it; the number of shareholders is somewhat smaller than is provided under this section.
It has a statutory meaning.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be glad to give consideration to the matter; but I think perhaps we had better let it stand for the moment. I would not want to make that decision this evening.

There is another point I should like to raise. On page 23-and it might be simpler to refer to the page and line number rather than the clause because of the fact that we are dealing with a group of them together-line 3 in subclause 4, we have a definition of "shareholder" for the purpose of these so-called private companies; and he is defined as "a person who is recorded on the books of the corporation as a shareholder". Has the minister given consideration to the position of the holders of bearer share warrants? It is obvious at once, of course, that

if you are going to include holders of bearer share warrants you would have to have some provision for the proof of the fact that the number of holders of bearer share warrants and registered shareholders combined does not exceed 75. But under this clause the minister reserves the right to make regulations and to set up the kind of proof that is required in determining the number of shareholders, and it does not seem to me to present too great a problem to define methods of proof in the case of holders of bearer share warrants.
Lest some hon. members be concerned about what might appear to be opening the door a little bit wider here, and lest they also be concerned perhaps as to the position of holders of bearer share warrants, for instance, under the succession duty act I should like to point out that there is no danger whatever in that respect. So far as this act is concerned, as I say, I think it should not be difficult to prove to the satisfaction of the department the number of holders of bearer share warrants. The number of shares is determined on the books of the company. The only point left to be determined would be the number of the holders. As long as proof is adduced to establish that the number of holders of bearer share warrants plus the number of registered shareholders does not exceed 75 in all, then it seems to me we should not be enacting legislation which is so restrictive in its terms as to exclude the holders of bearer share warrants.
On the succession duty angle may I point out that there is no possibility whatever of difficulty arising here. The shares of companies organized under the laws of this parliament or of any of the provinces have a situs or location in Canada for duty purposes, under section 6 (2) of the succession duty act. That section applies where the deceased died on or after January 1, 1948. Then under paragraph 2 of article III of the tax convention existing between Canada and the United States, for the avoidance of double taxation, we have a provision that the shares of Canadian companies shall be deemed to have situs in Canada; and it has been laid down that the fact that the shares are represented by bearer share warrants does not affect the position in the least. Under the succession duty act they are still deemed to have situs in Canada. Under the practice that exists, as I understand it, where the holder of bearer share warrants in a Canadian company dies in the United States, it is the practice of the United States government to report that fact to the Canadian government, and succession duty is levied in Canada

in that case. A similar practice prevails in the converse case where the holder in Canada of bearer shares in a United States corporation dies here. I ask the minister's consideration of that point because bearer share warrants are a useful means of evidencing ownership of the shares of a corporation. I submit that this provision is unduly restrictive in its present form; that it could be widened without risk.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will give some consideration to that. As my hon. friend knows, the use of bearer share warrants is extremely rare, certainly in the case of private companies. I had a reasonably extensive practice in matters of this kind and I can think of only three or four companies that use them. The Canadian Pacific issue share warrants, the Imperial Oil and the International Petroleum used to; but they are very rare in the case of private companies. I knew of no case of less than seventy-five; but if there is any hardship I shall certainly look into it. We are going to proceed a little cautiously with this section. It is not a section of general application to companies which are widely held, but I shall take note of my hon. friend's suggestion, and perhaps if we are reviewing the section next year, to extend it to give it somewhat wider scope, we will bring in the question of share warrants.

Do I take it that in the
regulations that the minister proposes to lay down under this section determining the terms of proof it is proposed to include the holders of bearer share warrants?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If we can do it legally it
could be considered. It would seem to me that perhaps it would be the sort of thing one should spell out in the act. I will think it over.

I want to go back to section 11, because I still want to persuade the minister that the point I am raising there is a point that, purely by reason of wording, a narrow construction may be given which quite possibly is never intended.
I	want to go back and repeat what I said before. At the present time, under section
II	it applies only to the simple case apparently of where one company is acquired by another. It would operate unfairly, I suggest, in the case of a company having several subsidiaries or even sub-subsidiaries. I want to suggest to the minister again that it would be entirely in accordance with the spirit of this legislation if a broader interpretation were given. I am suggesting that the section be amended to provide that it is not to apply (1) to the case where the company acquiring the shares already controls through
Income Tax Act
the ownership of shares of another company the company whose shares are transferred. The minister will appreciate that that is a method of acquiring control, not in the simple way indicated in the section but in a more complicated way, but nevertheless the relationship is the same, I submit; (2) to a case where the company acquiring the shares and the company whose shares are acquired are controlled directly or indirectly by the same company. I suggest to the minister these two cases are entirely within the four corners of the section but owing to the naryow wording of the section they might be shut out. The section says simply and exclusively that it applies to cases where control of one company first of all is acquired -that is not the wording of the section- where one company is acquired by another. That is the effect of it. Will the minister not give consideration to that right now and say whether what I am suggesting is reasonable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whether I have been able to think through exactly what my hon. friend is suggesting. He appreciates that this section does not apply to any acquisition of control, by subsidiary or further subsidiary or anything else, entered into prior to the 10th of May, 1950. It is only for the future. Offhand I must say that the evil that we are attempting to correct here could be achieved by going through two or three transfers just as readily as it could by making one.
I am suggesting that this is substantially the same as what the minister has in mind. Will the minister let this section stand until he has time to consider it? Surely that is a reasonable request?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that the case to which my hon. friend is referring has been considered, and we felt that the evil which we are trying to prevent could be avoided in that way; that one company which controls another and which has a surplus could sell these shares to another subsidiary at the book value, and in that way get the surplus out tax free without paying the tax which we think should be imposed.

Mr. Chairman, the expression "resident" and the expression "non-resident" as applied to corporations and as used here in various places are not defined. There is no definition to determine residence in the section. What basis does the department propose to follow to determine residence in the case of a corporation? Are they going by head office?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand that the rule which is followed is laid down in the British

Income Tax Act
Columbia Electric case. Stated rather briefly, where the seat of management and control of the corporation rests constitutes the residence for the purposes of the act.

In the administration of the act will a corporation be treated as having only one residence? After all, there are many cases where a corporation may have its head office, its management offices, in one country and still be carrying on very substantial operations in the other country. There are a good many of these cases on either side of the international boundary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend will recognize that they can have only one residence for purposes of our tax. There are a good many Canadian companies that do business in the United States, and a good many United States companies that do business here through either branches or subsidiaries. If they do business through branches then the reciprocal arrangements both of the tax treaty and the act apply, and there are appropriate provisions for credits of taxes paid in the other country. I do not think any difficulty has arisen in practice under the act so far as I am aware.
Mr. Chairman, I have a technical amendment to section 28 which I am told is merely to correct a drafting error. Perhaps my colleague the Minister of Agriculture would move it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I move:
That clause 28 be amended by substituting the word Part for the word "Act" in subparagraph (ii) of paragraph (a) of section 73A of the Act, by substituting "1949" for "1950" in subparagraph (iv) of the same paragraph; by substituting the words "reduced previous to the specified year" for the words "previously reduced" in subparagraph (v) of the same paragraph, and by substituting the words "subsection (4) of section 73" for the words "section 73" in subparagraph (i) of paragraph (b) of subsection (1) of section 73A.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have a second amendment to the section which includes section 73B, relating to mining, which I would ask my colleague to move.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I move:
That clause 28 be amended by substituting the following subsection for subsection (4) of section 73B:
" (4) Paragraph (b) of subsection (2) and paragraph (b) of subsection (3) do not apply:
(a)	in the case of a person who disposes of the shares after carrying on a campaign to sell shares of the corporation to the public, or
(b)	to shares acquired by the exercise of an option to purchase shares received as consideration for property described in paragraph (a) of subsection (2) or paragraph (a) of subsection (3)."
I do not know whether the minister wants to make a statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I should make a brief statement. I assumed that some hon. members would wish to discuss this section. The amendment which is proposed here is to give statutory recognition to a practice which has prevailed since 1941 in the income tax administration with respect to persons who invest or put moneys into the location and development of mining properties. I am informed that in 1941 a directive was issued by 'the then deputy minister of income tax in which he provided, in substance, what is set out in this section, namely, that if I alone or in conjunction with others put $10,000 or $15,000 into locating a mining claim, and had done a certain amount of preliminary work in proving up the property, locating it and so on, and then sell that claim for a substantial profit, either in cash or in shares, that profit will not be taxable-even though I may make a business of doing that, day after day, month after month, or year after year.
It was felt it was desirable to give statutory recognition to an administrative practice which, frankly, I thought the terms of the law scarcely justified. In this section, as it originally appeared in the bill, we had provided that a person would not be eligible for that special consideration if he were engaged in carrying on a business of dealing with the public in shares and securities. On reconsideration it did not seem fair to me that because a man was a stock broker or a bond dealer, or even if he was a mining stock broker, he should be precluded from making this type of investment, or doing this type of promotional work, just because of the fact that he might make his livelihood out of underwriting shares and selling them.
That is the purpose of the amendment which has just been read and, briefly, the purpose of the section. There is rjo change whatever in the law as it has been administered since 1941. However, the section I am proposing gives statutory recognition to this special extent in favour of those people who back the promotion of development by the location and the development of mining properties.

I am glad to have the minister's statement in this matter because, as he knows, there has been some considerable worry about this section. As the minister knows, the financing, discovery and development of a mine is an extremely hazardous and speculative business. Unless every encouragement is given both to individuals and to companies engaged in this extremely hazardous and speculative business we will not find that this type of capital,

this speculative capital, so essential for the development of mines, will continue but that it will tend to dry up.
The minister would be infernally lucky if he were on the ground floor in respect of even one producing mine. If he took a number of speculative chances he would find that the number of times he does win or that he does get in on the ground floor would be extremely rare. Over the past quarter century I believe the chances are less than one per cent.
I mention this merely to show how necessary it is to encourage risk capital in the development of mines. I understand the reason for this amendment. In many ways I have some sympathy for the purpose indicated by the minister. But there is grave danger in any attempt to restrict individuals who, to put it colloquially, make a practice of taking bets in the development of mines.
Some of us do it, to our sorrow, in an amateurish sort of way. But the net result is frequently, and more or less generally, unsuccessful. Some of us who perhaps have more time and more knowledge consider that it is part of a necessary development of the Canadian economy. Even so, despite the knowledge we have, and the trouble and exploration involved, we also find that the secrets of nature are very, very elusive. Even though a mine or an ore body is discovered-and this is not a common thing- and reasonably delimited by diamond drilling, trenching or shaft sinking, then we have the great difficulty of raising capital to develop what is considered, from engineering judgment, to be a worth-while ore body.
There is no easier way to kill the mining industry than to restrict speculation. By its very nature mining is an extremely speculative business. Even though you have what you consider to be a rich ore body, as indicated by surface drilling, until that rich ore body is developed, cross-cuts put through it, stopes developed, and shafts and mills erected, you have not got a mine; and all the work, all the effort and all the capital put into this may go for naught.
May I emphasize to the minister that to restrict in any way the flow of speculative capital into mining in its early stages is going to do the greatest disservice to the development of this country that could be done by anyone. Mining is entirely different from ordinary business. In ordinary business procedure, particularly manufacturing, a prospectus is issued, on which there is a reasonable estimate as to the probable profit that can be made. In mining no such thing occurs. All one can do is to say, "We have such-and-such a property; the geology is such-and-such;
Income Tax Act
we have diamond-drilled it and found that we have such-and-such an intersection carrying such-and-such a value." On that bet, and only on that bet, does the initial speculator put money into the property.
That is an extremely hazardous and extremely speculative bet. But that is where mines are made. It is that type of speculation, that type of gambling, if we wish so to describe it colloquially, that gives the prospector and the initial developer and the man who puts up the money for the diamond drilling and the man who puts up the money for the initial trenching or the geophysical work or for the initial shaft-sinking, the money to go ahead with the development of the mine. As I have said, the betting against such capital is about a hundred to one but it is still a hundred to one. If by any regulation you make the one per cent who are a success subject to taxation for income purposes you are going to kill the goose that laid the golden egg more surely than by anything else that could be done to destroy the development of our country. I hope what the minister has said is correct, and that the section in fact does what he has said it does, namely, encourages the investment of capital in the mining business.
There are two or three cases which I think should be brought to the attention of the committee. In mining there are groups of prospectors who form themselves into syndicates. Then there are companies whose principal business is concerned with the prospecting and developing of mining properties. The act merely deals with prospectors as individuals. As a matter of fact most prospecting is done by syndicates at the present time. The old-fashioned individual prospector is very nearly a thing of the past. A great deal of prospecting is done by companies making a specialty of such work. I should like a statement from the minister to the effect that the capital gains, which may occasionally accrue to syndicates and prospecting companies that are fortunate enough to discover a property and develop it to the stage where its stock can be sold publicly, will not be taxed. I should like an assurance that the profit of the original prospector, whether it be an individual, syndicate or company, will be considered as a capital gain and not taxable even though the prospecting syndicate is principally engaged in the business of prospecting and carrying on the early development of mining properties.	*

Will the minister give the committee the assurance that the intent and meaning of subsection 3 of section 73B is the same as that in the departmental ruling of 1941?

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am told the departmental ruling of 1941 took the form of a directive from the then deputy minister of taxation. I am also told that the section as drafted sets out exactly the practice that the department has been following since that time. I cannot make that statement from my own personal knowledge because I do not administer that department. As I said at the outset, there is no intention in this section to change in any way the practice which has prevailed since 1941.
The hon. member for York West raised the question as to what the position would be with respect to a syndicate. If the syndicate is unincorporated it obviously comes straight within the specific language of the section. If the development work was done by means of the purchase of shares in what was loosely referred to as a syndicate, then the ordinary rules with respect to the purchase of shares would apply, and the question whether or not there would be tax liability would depend on the quality of the investor.

That is just the question. Frequently a syndicate or individual will invest money in a prospect by taking down shares either in a syndicate or in an incorporated company. Many companies today have been incorporated and then several other development companies have purchased stock in the incorporated company-I am thinking of one particularly-in order to advance development. Let us take a mine which is one of the most active presently in the Canadian economy, and which may develop into a major copper producer. I will not mention its name but many members probably know it. It requires several million dollars to bring it into production. Several companies have invested large sums of money in this one company by the purchase of treasury stock. That money went immediately, without any deduction, into the development of the property which as yet is unproven.
It will take probably a year or so and possibly three or four million dollars more to decide definitely whether it is a major commercial operation. At the present time several prospecting companies whose business it is to develop mines have purchased stock in company X, shall we say, in order to put money in the treasury to enable company X to be developed. There is a strong possibility that a mine will be developed on the property. If that happens it may be that the individual companies which have invested money to bring company X into production will wish to sell a part or all of their equity in the producing mine a year or two years from now. I want to ask the minister

whether the money so received is going to be considered as income of these companies or as capital gain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As my hon. friend has put it, I would say it would not be subject to tax. If one or two companies then proceeded to make a market for the stock, underwrite the stock and increase the capital of the company after it had been proven there was a producing mine, then of course they would be engaged in another operation. On the facts as set out, however, if two or three of them invested in a prospect, brought it to the point where it got to be a real mine and then sold their stock to somebody else, they would come within the operation of this section and in my opinion would not be subject to tax.
It is a fine distinction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are fine distinctions in all these cases; it cannot be helped. There are always cases in which it is very hard to tell whether a man is making an ordinary investment or speculation, or whether he is engaging in a regular course of dealing which constitutes a business.
The size of the chancellor's boot, as you and I used to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is about it.
If this section is not clarified to the satisfaction of those interested in mining development, I am afraid it will seriously affect the development of new properties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would hope that the explanation I have given this evening would go a long way toward reassuring those people, and toward clearing up what I think has been some misunderstanding of the real situation. I repeat, there is no change whatever in the existing law. Rather there is a change in the existing law, because I think a practice has been prevailing since 1945 which was not justified by law, and we are now making legal what I think was of questionable validity under the ruling to which I have referred.
That is the ruling of 1941?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I realize what the minister is trying to do in this section, and I appreciate his intentions; but there has been a very considerable amount of worry in the legitimate mining business over this section, and I know the minister has received representations from people who are interested in prospecting and developing. That is why I

want it abundantly clear that there is no intention to tax as income any profit made from the development by a mining company or a mining syndicate of a worth-while prospect which is subsequently sold to the public and becomes a public company. That is so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I did not follow my hon. friend very closely, but I answered him previously. On the facts he set up before, if an individual, a corporation or anybody else backs a new development, brings it to the mining stage and sells it, the profit on that transaction, even if he makes a habit of doing that sort of thing, is not taxable.
Even if it was an incorporated company before he did it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
Many companies are up against it for capital today-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the case of shares it would have to qualify as a speculation or investment, not as a marketing operation. But there would not be any objection to a mining company buying shares in an incorporated prospect, thereby providing the prospect with the cash to go ahead and do the development. Then if the prospect turned out to be a mine it could sell the shares and take that profit. That would be a capital profit. Of course, in the case I have cited, if they engaged in a marketing operation, took up options on additional stock and made a market for it, then what I have said would have no application.
Thank you very much; I think that is clear.

I shall ask one of my colleagues to move that section 32, subsection 1, be amended by striking out the words May 4, 1950, in subsection 3 of section 95A and replacing them by the words May 10, 1950.

On section 37-Interest.

I should like to mention a matter in connection with the imposition of interest. This is not by way of quarrelling with this section, because I am sure it will commend itself to the house since it involves a reduction in the rate of interest in this particular case from 7 per cent to 6 per cent. However, this gives me an opportunity to say that I think the Department of National Revenue is going unwarrantably far in imposing interest in the case of taxpayers who pay their current income tax on a quarterly basis, which means they estimate their income. I have seen one or two cases lately in which it seems to me the department has taken an attitude that is simply indefensible in insisting on charging interest on the balance required to be paid by a taxpayer who has made an estimate and who, after making his four quarterly payments, finds that his estimate was too low and so has a substantial payment to make on April 30 following. It seems to me that in the case of persons coming within that classification, people who make an estimate of their income and their tax and on that estimate make-quarterly payments on their tax, the department has no business to expect them to do-almost superhuman things in refining the estimate of their income. There are many people in that category who by March 31 cannot even come close to estimating their income for the year, and I submit as strongly as I can that in cases of that kind the department has no business at all imposing interest charges.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend will appreciate that this only applies to 1948 and previous years. The law in that respect has now been changed, but that was the law that applied in those years. The obligation was upon the taxpayer to estimate, and if he underestimated the interest penalty ensued.

Income Tax Act

Quite so, but I am taking advantage of this opportunity to complain about the way that provision is being administered at the present time. While I appreciate that it is the Department of National Revenue and not that of finance, I do register a very strong protest against what I consider to be harsh administration.

On section 46-Deductions from income of corporation in petroleum or natural gas business.

I have a few remarks I
should like to make on this section, and a few questions I should like to ask. I am glad to see there has been a remarkable increase in interest in, and knowledge of, oil and gas development, particularly by people in eastern Canada, during the last two or three years. I have noticed it particularly, because in travelling across the country, when I tell people I come from Alberta they immediately start talking about the oil business; that was not the case a few short years ago. I think by now we all recognize the advantages to Canada of extensive oil and gas exploration and drilling programs. During the past two or three years we have had fairly extensive programs of that kind.
I should like to make the point that the taxation structure should be such as to encourage oil and gas men to further extend that program. I do not think there is any need to go into the advantages of that. If Canada becomes self sufficient in oil it means that the tremendous saving of United States dollars would go a long way towards fighting our generally adverse balance of trade with that nation. There are a number of misconceptions which are common about the oil and gas business. A large number of people have the idea that all you have to do in Alberta is dig a hole any place, and you immediately get a gusher and are wealthy for the rest of your life. When some of the people I meet find I

am from Alberta they say, "Do you own an oil well?" I have to admit with sorrow that I do not own an oil well. They seem to be surprised that anyone who comes from Alberta does not own one. The general idea seems to be that everyone in Alberta is wealthy and owns an oil or gas well, and there is no trouble about getting one. That is so far from the truth, it should not be necessary to say much about it, but I should like to put on the record a few figures to show what an extremely hazardous industry the oil industry is, and covering the profits which have accrued to people in that industry.
I have a compilation of the expenditures of twelve of the largest oil companies now operating in Alberta, and who have been operating there for a year or more. This shows what their returns have been up to date. These twelve companies have expended in exploration work, acquiring acreage for drilling and general operating costs-this excludes completely all costs of refining and relates to the expenditures incurred in the search for oil- $287,912,000. During that same period their gross return, which they received for the oil, amounted to $156,188,000, after they had subtracted from that the payment of royalties. In other words, they have spent the sum of $130 million more in the search for oil than they received for the oil which they found. I believe that is a good indication of the fact that this oil business has not been all gravy. It is not the easiest thing in the world to get
oil.	On the contrary, it is a very difficult thing. In the United States the general average of productive wells drilled is about one in five. There are four dry holes to one well which produces. Up to date in Canada it has been closer to twenty-three or twenty-four dry holes to one producing well.
A lot of people answer this by saying that a number of these companies have only been operating in the exploration and drilling business in Canada for a comparatively short time, and therefore you cannot take figures such as I have been giving as being indicative of the profit. I should like, therefore, to separate from the figures I have given the figures for the two companies which have been in operation there for the longest period of time, Imperial Oil Limited and its former subsidiary, Royalite Oil Company. During their entire period of operation these two companies, which were formerly one, have expended nearly $160 million, and they have received in return for that just over $111 million. These two companies, which have been in business the longest and have had producing wells for a long time in the Turner valley, have spent up to date roughly $48 million more than they received. Now, that gives an indication of the risky nature of

this business, and the fact that large sums have to be expended on exploration work before any returns are secured.
In view of that fact, I should like to make the point that during what is really the exploration period, so far as the development of the oil fields in Canada is concerned, and that is the period in which we are now, that exploration work should be burdened as little as possible by taxation costs which hamper operations. These costs prevent the companies from drilling as many wells as they might drill otherwise.
Coming to specific points in connection with this particular section, I should like the minister to clarify these bonus payments and other acquisition costs. In a brief submitted to the minister on February 21, 1950, the western Canada petroleum association asked that those bonus payments, and other acquisition costs in connection with securing leases, be allowed as expenses when the property had to be abandoned as unproductive. These expenses did not result in anything of capital value accruing to the company. As such they should be included as exploration expenses, the same as the costs of the geophysical survey. In so far as I can interpret this amendment, there is nothing in it to take care of costs of this kind. What is the situation in connection with these costs? Are they going to be allowed under these amendments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The answer to that is that this amendment excludes those costs. They cannot be amortized, but the depletion is permitted against it. My hon. friend is referring to the bonus payments, those payments that you bid for?

Yes. I should like to suggest to the minister that costs of that kind, where no producing well has been brought in and where they do not represent any gain to the company whatever, should be allowed as an exploration cost or development cost, the same as other costs are.
My next question is this. In the explanatory note I see the following:
Subclause (1). The new subsection (1) corrects a technical error in the existing subsection.
What is the technical error that is corrected?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The words "the lesser of" were inadvertently omitted in the section as it now appears.

Can the minister tell us what difference that makes? In other words, what is the effect of this change going to be?
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The amendment is to section 53 (1), and that section as it now stands reads as follows:
A corporation whose principal business is production, refining or marketing of petroleum, petroleum products or natural gas or exploring or drilling for petroleum or natural gas may deduct in computing its income, for the purposes of The Income Tax Act, the lesser of.
Those words "the lesser of" were left out by accidental means; it was perhaps not quite a typographical error but about as close to that as possible. And then it goes on:
(a) the aggregate of the drilling and exploration costs . . .
And so on. On reading the section it becomes quite clear that you need such words as "the lesser of" in order to make it comprehensible.
Do I take it that the putting in of those words is going to make things less favourable for the oil companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no. It is just to give the section meaning, which it did not have before.

The explanatory note also states:
Subclause (2). The new subsection (2A) provides a deduction for so-called "lease rentals" up to $1 per acre for 1949 and later years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the clause that excludes the bonus payments that my hon. friend was referring to.
Yes. As I understand it the lease rentals expenditure, as it is called, of $1 an acre is allowed as an income tax deduction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would not be without this section, but it is with this section.

No, but with this section it will allow it. If the lease rental is $5 an acre, as I understand it, $1 of this would be allowed as a deductible expense but the other $4 per acre would not be allowed as a deductible expense. Is that correct? I understand that it does not matter really what the amount of that lease rental is per acre, that allowance will be made only up to $1. It might be $10 per acre.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If it were an annual rental and exceeded $1 per year, only $1 would be allowed.

Yes. It does not matter whether it is $5, $6 or what it is; the $1 is still allowed. That is the point I was getting at.
Next I should like to ask what the situation is in a case in which prepayment of this lease rental has taken place. For example, there are many individual freehold owners

Income Tax Act
of mineral rights, and they will give a rental only for a period of years, say for ten years or something of that kind. If, for example, the rental was only $1 a year, they would give a lease rental on a basis of a 10-year lease, at $1 a year; but they would give it only if they were paid the entire amount when the lease was entered into. In other words, they would have to get the $10 per acre at the start.
The reason for that is quite simple. There are many people who go into the oil business, and they would enter into contracts of this kind. They might have bad luck and put down a number of dry holes. The result is that the company would go broke. Then the man who had given this 10-year lease would of course have no means of collecting the money. In order therefore to ensure that he does collect the money, in many cases-and I think in the majority of cases-he wants to get the money when the lease is entered into. When that situation exists, when there is a prepayment of this lease rental will the deduction be allowed at the rate of $1 for say the ten years in this case that we instanced that the lease lasts?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: 1 would hesitate to answer that question on a hypothetical basis. I think you would have to look at the agreement. Under certain conditions, if it were a genuine prepayment and so on, it could perhaps be allowed or spread over the period. But I would have to see the agreement before I would feel free to give a definite answer.
By that does the minister mean that what you might call discretion will have to be exercised in each individual case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. It would depend on the facts. There is the law. The law says:
(2A) In computing a deduction under subsection (1) or (2) no amount shall be included in respect of a payment for or in respect of a right, licence or privilege to explore for, drill for or take petroleum or natural gas other than an annual payment not exceeding $1 per acre.
That is clear enough. There is nothing obscure about that language. That would have to be applied to the particular contract which was entered into.
I think it is very obscure. Suppose it is a 10-year job and they paid for that all at once. Why do you not say they are allowed to deduct that?

I think that the case I gave was quite clear. If prepayment had been made for ten years, shall the $1 an acre which had been paid all at once to cover the 10-year period be deducted year by year at the rate of $1 per acre?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would have to look at it when the circumstances came up.

I do not know, but it would seem to me that as this will actually operate in practice, the interpretation which is going to be placed upon it is perhaps the most important thing. I should think that the minister could make that a little bit clearer for the benefit of the oil people involved.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I have had to say in this chamber before, Mr. Chairman, I used to charge for opinions of that kind, but I cannot do so now. I will therefore leave it to my other colleagues at the bar who earn their living in that way.
I should like to ask the minister this question. Is a payment such as that in the hands of the recipient, say the farmer who gets it, considered as income in his hands, or is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would depend on the circumstances of the case. I would think if it is an annual payment of so much an acre, it would be income. That is only a personal opinion, offhand; and free.

It is considered as income. I would make the proposition that it should certainly be allowed on the $1 an acre basis over the ten years or fifteen years or whatever period the lease might last for.
I should like to go on to another point now, and that is the question of reservation and extension fees for these reservations. In the province of Alberta when an oil company applies to the Alberta government it secures what is known as an oil reservation which gives them the right to prospect for oil or to survey it and explore for oil on it. The normal payment for that I think is $250. That covers the reservation for the first year. Then the second year the company holds this reservation they get an extension as it is called; and the second year they pay 30 cents an acre for the right to explore on that land. If they wish to continue to explore on it a third year, they pay 70 cents an acre during the third year. I should like to ask if payments of that kind are included under this subsection 2A. In other words, are these reservation fees and extension fees allowable as part of the $1 per acre which is provided for in this amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that if they are annual payments, they would come under this section. I cannot speak from personal knowledge.

I think these reservation and extension fees, as I have indicated, are annual payments. I think that your adviser, Dr. Eaton, could advise you in connection

with that. I think he knows much more about that than anybody else here. He knows much more about this than anybody else.
I would take it then that companies of that kind are included. Can the minister say definitely whether they are included or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am basing my statement on information which I have received from officials that if they are on annual payment they would come under the section which we are discussing.
Then there are certain other fees.
The minister is not charging for that opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; these are all free opinions.
I must say that in some of these opinions the minister is not committing himself very firmly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not want to infringe the prerogatives of the legal profession.

I do not like to see so many loopholes left or opened up. The next question I should like to ask is in connection with lease agents' fees and legal expenses. When an oil company starts looking for leases it very frequently gets them from a lease agent whose business it is to pick up leases and to handle them as an agent might handle real estate or anything else. The ordinary fee paid to a lease agent runs anywhere from 10 cents an acre to a dollar an acre. And of course there are certain legal expenses in connection with securing leases. Unfortunately these legal expenses always seem to creep up, and in some instances they come to a considerable amount. Are these lease agents' fees and legal expenses incurred in connection with securing a lease applicable to this dollar an acre business?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not familiar with that business, Mr. Chairman, but they sound like capital expenditures to me.
Lawyers' fees?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

When did you
find that out?

I should like to point out that lease agents' fees or legal fees are as much of an expense to the company which is in the oil exploring and drilling business as any other sort of expense; and if they cannot be applied under this dollar an acre clause, then I would contend that they should be applicable under section 4, I think it is, which provides for exploration and other expenses being deducted. Will the minister
Income Tax Act
tell me whether any of these things are deductible under what you might call general exploration expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot give any general opinion, but legal fees are a capital expense. If they are legal fees, for instance, incurred in acquiring a piece of immovable property, or if you hire a lawyer to examine title to a factory that you wish to purchase, it is a part of the capital cost of the factory.
I suppose if you incurred some legal fees for the purpose of getting a lease it may be part of your leasing cost. I am speaking with a great deal of diffidence here because I know nothing about the way in which the oil business is conducted or how the lawyers who advise the oil companies or the lessees charge.
I know that I am in the presence of experts here in that line, so I am speaking with a great deal of caution.

Section 4 provides that all expenses incurred directly or indirectly in searching for minerals in Canada are deductible. My contention is that this type of expense is one which is not indirectly, it is really directly, incurred in order to be able to search for oil, and to take part in the search for oil, and as such it should be deductible. Under the regulations I think it comes down to departmental rulings. If the present departmental ruling does not include expenses of this sort I would urge upon the minister that it be changed so that they are included either in subsection 2A or subsection 4. It does not matter under which section it is put except that I think it would be better under section 4.
The next matter that I should like to deal with is surface rental costs. I do not see anything in either of these sections covering surface rental expenses. I understand in the past it has been ruled by the department that these surface rental expenses are not deductible as operating expenses. Why that should be I quite fail to understand. The situation is this, Mr. Chairman. In Alberta when an oil company goes on a man's land, what is known as an arbitration board sits on the case and determines what compensation that man, the owner of the surface rights, shall be paid for the inconvenience caused him by the oil drilling company going on his land and taking some of it out of production and, I suppose, for the right of entry and things along that line.
In Alberta the ordinary amount which has been awarded by the arbitration board has been between $1,200 and $1,500 per well site. In other words every time a company drills a well it has to pay the surface owner $1,200 to $1,500 for the right to drill. It has nothing

Income Tax Act
to do with the minerals underneath. In addition to that the arbitration board fixes the rental a year for the area around the well. The area taken is usually four acres, and for that four acres the usual arbitration award has run from $65 to $100 an acre. In other words, up to $400 a year is paid as surface rental for the four acres that surround the well site. This of course could not possibly apply under the dollar an acre business because the cost per acre is so much greater that it would have no effect, really.
Has consideration been given to looking at these expenses as normal exploration or drilling expenses? It is certainly an ordinary drilling expense, in my opinion. The minister said a while ago that anything that went on from year to year could be included in the dollar an acre provision, and so forth. This is a thing that goes on from year to year as long as the well is producing, and it seems to me it should be included as a legitimate expense for the production of oil. Can the minister make a statement on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That particular point about rental for surface rights has not been brought to my attention so far as I am aware. I have listened to my hon. friend's remarks, and I shall ask the Department of National Revenue to see how they are dealing with it. I presume it must have been brought to their attention, but it was not included in the brief that the western petroleum-
Yes, it was included in their brief-in fact I am quite sure it was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not in the brief submitted to me. However, I will look into the question.

The minister has mentioned the brief which was submitted by the western Canada petroleum association. In the past he has given favourable consideration to many of the recommendations which have been made by that association, which takes in all of the oil men engaged in exploring and drilling for oil in western Canada. What reception was given to or what decision was made on the recommendations that they submitted to him this year? We have already dealt with some of them, but in addition to that there is their recommendation that depletion be calculated on the basis of the income from each individual well or property instead of against all the wells of the company, after charging against such well or property only the cost directly attributed to it. What was done in connection with that, if anything?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I had a very pleasant interview with representatives of the association. Careful consideration was given to their representations, and such of those representations as it was possible to implement will be found in the sections of the bill. It was not found possible to accept their request that depletion be calculated on individual well basis.

Another matter which I
have brought up here year after year, and which is contained as the third recommendation of this association, is that the deduction of drilling and exploration costs be put on a permanent basis. It was put on a three-year basis, and it has been extended for another year; or is it proposed to extend it by this act? I asked the parliamentary assistant about this when we were dealing with the resolution, and he said he understood considerable attention had been given to it but it had not been decided to make a change this year. I wonder if the minister can add anything to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What the parliamentary assistant said is correct. We did not feel that we could yet put this very special provision on a permanent basis, but we have now put it on a three-year basis. They know three years ahead what the provision will be. At a later date it may be possible to carry out that recommendation which has been made, but I do not feel we can do it this year.

I was glad when it was put on the three-year basis last year, and I am glad to find that that has been extended another year. I would hope further consideration would be given to it before the next budget is brought down, so that these various special deductions for oil and gas drilling companies might be put on a permanent basis, so that they would know where they stand and so that as a result of that provision they could lay out a ten-year program, or whatever it seemed wisest to do, always knowing their exact position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

only to companies the main business of which is that of drilling for oil. It is considered out in that country that there are probably quite a number of mining companies with money available to them who, if these special deductions were extended to them, would go into the drilling business.

I do not wish to repeat all I have said.

My question is this: What consideration has been given to placing all taxpayers who drill for gas and oil, even though that is not their main business, on the same basis as oil companies, so far as gas and oil operations are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My recollection is that we began giving consideration to that back in 1943 or 1944, when I was parliamentary assistant to the then minister of finance, and we decided we should not do it. Our mind has not changed since then.
Then, section 73 of the Income Tax Act-

It has been repealed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I am glad that is so. I believe that will assist in the exploration program by making it possible to finance a considerable number of wells by means of royalty trusts, which otherwise could not have been financed. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the section carry?

No. I shall keep the committee for less than five minutes. But in dealing with all these sections and subsections I believe it is apparent that the government has lost the idea in connection with the general policy with respect to the development of oil in the country from which I come. What it should be-and the minister may tell me that this is the policy-is that, first, the government should not be inclined to collect
Income Tax Act
income tax, except from those people who have earned an income. That is a very gentle statement of the situation; but I think perhaps it is a proper basis upon which to consider the matter.
I agree with the details mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary East-and do not regard that lightly, because we have talked the matter over in our room. Here is what, it seems to me, should have been done: the history of the industry indicates, and it is admitted by all of us, that the development of oil in Canada is a very important development indeed. I must assume that any government in Canada will do all it can to assist in that development, having in mind the benefit which will be derived by the whole of the country.
One need mention only the dollar situation to realize the significance of this. I am sure the minister will appreciate what I have in mind. My objection to what is being done is that the government has lost sight of the general benefits the country should have from this industry, and it is stumbling over little bits of things which, in terms of revenue to the country, mean very little. Yet, to the individual or company confronted with these things, they constitute stumbling blocks greater in extent than might have been envisaged by those who prepared them.
Let us refer to one point mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary East-and perhaps to only one. We approach the man who owns his own oil rights, having secured those rights back in the nineties. He is in the position of being on a wildcat acreage, in possession of a half-section. He says to the leasehound- those are the fellows who are always wanting to be regarded as exceptions, but you do not worry much about them-"a dollar an acre?- yes. You will not be here for some years, will you?" They say No. I am being very practical about this, because there are not nearly enough drilling outfits in the world to permit those companies operating under permit to conform with the conditions set out by the Alberta government. That is the reason we hear about farm-outs. Imperial Oil will see this company and that company on a split basis of return-farm-outs-in order to carry out the program.
This man says, "I am not going to give you a lease on my property for ten years at one dollar an acre, payable year by year,"-which in wildcat country is probably the going rate. He says, "If you will give me ten times $320, then I will talk to you. I will give it to you on the dollar-a-year basis, but I want cash in my little hot hand right now."

Income Tax Act
Under the present legislation the company, which pays him not $320, but ten times that, may on that basis deduct only one dollar an acre, or $320. At the same time the Department of National Revenue takes from the man who gave the company the lease, with prepayment over a ten-year period, income tax in that one year for all the money he got. Let us have a little bit of consistency about this matter. It is income in the hands of the recipient, and what is the situation with respeot to the man who pays it? I go a step further. I am merely making suggestions, and I am not being tough about the matter. If we were back on the question of depreciation I could be very tough. I notice that the minister and the man who invented this cock-eyed depreciation are having a little chat at the moment.
What I say is that we should promote the purpose which the government has, which it must have, and for which I honour them. They are seeking the development of oil, and we all want that to take place. It seems to me that when it comes down to a question of charging an expense to make that development the department might even adopt an attitude of generosity. You should talk to Dr. Hume about it. It involves so much and so many things. An attitude of generosity would not hurt at all the development which is going on out there. With great respect, may I say that is not your attitude. Your position is that you have allowed implements such as drilling equipment to enter Canada from the United States duty free. You thought you had given somebody a great Christmas present. All you did was to give Canada a chance to develop. In dollars you have got it back a thousandfold. I am sick and tired of being told that last year you gave so much and this year you will give a little more. Why not make one bite of the cherry and simply say that expenses incurred in exploration will be allowed, particularly if they result in dry wells or non-productive areas. Let us quit quibbling about the matter and put an end to it by adopting that view. [DOT] I know that in several other departments of federal and provincial governments such as workmen's compensation and unemployment insurance instructions have gone out that if a question of doubt arises it should be resolved in favour of the individual.
That is not the position with respect to the oil business. The oil business is not begging. These people, if their ideas of development are correct, will come out all right at the end of the road. When they do they will not mind the government imposing income tax to whatever extent the government thinks reasonable, but they do object to taxes being imposed on them now. With the greatest respect in the world to Dr. Eaton,
[Mr. Smith (Calgary West).!
they are being imposed on companies searching for oil even when the results of their searches are fruitless. Let us take one of the instances referred to by the hon. member for Calgary East. In the great generosity of your big hearts you have allowed $1 an acre. Suppose you cannot get the land for $1 an acre. Suppose it costs you $10 an acre. You drill the land and you lose your money. You have paid $10 an acre, and it is not much satisfaction to know that you are allowed $1.
In saying that I come back to the point that your purpose must be to encourage the finding and development of oil in Canada. I have enunciated your broad policy for you perhaps too generously but it is what you are.doing in these small picayune ways. It is the pinpricks. You are using $1 an acre against $2 an acre and all that sort of nonsense. When a man pays $10 for a ten-year period $1 an acre will be his but the $9 is not. That sort of thing will not develop the oil business in Canada. I am not going to use harsh language. Oil development is taking place in spite of restrictions. I want to thank Dr. Eaton and the other persons with whom the oil people have had to deal for fair treatment within the knowledge which Dr. Eaton had supported by the knowledge given to him by those persons who call on him. Let us stop worrying in this House of Commons about $2 here and there. By proper encouragement and not picking on these people we will get $2,000 for every dollar we have been bothering about.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, it is an attitude that I am talking about. I am not dealing with any of the details which have been touched upon. I wish Dr. Eaton would come to Alberta and I would drive him around to some of these places. There is oil in Alberta and in neighbouring provinces because it is not going to be confined to Alberta. Let us remember that within the past week the government sold two quarter-sections, only 160 acres each, for $3,188,000 by way of bonus allowance.
Just the oil rights.

Only the rights and that by way of a bonus. They still have their $1 an acre, and perhaps it has put that figure into the minds of some people here. They still have 12J per cent of the gross. That means that for every barrel of oil that comes out of the ground they will receive one-eighth. Let us get that idea into our minds. We are not dealing with little piddling things. I speak from a dominion standpoint. The minister is happy. He thought that some of the radio broadcasts he made straightened out the dollar situation.

Income Tax Act
With great respect, Alberta did more to straighten out the dollar situation than all the radio talks the minister ever made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A few other things helped besides Alberta.
Pardon?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Alberta was very helpful but there were other things that helped besides, apart from the radio talks.

Rich Albertans stopped travelling. I think that was one of the things that happened, and those who were not rich never travelled anyway. Let us get down to cases and not talk a lot of nonsense about people going to Florida. Let us all grasp this vision. For all the dollars you are going to get by the few things mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary East, it will cost you more to collect them than you will have at the end of the year.
Let us think of this. We all agree on the development of industry within our country. We all say production is the only thing that can carry us, that production is the only thing that can carry a $2,400 million budget. I hope I am right in that figure. It not only staggered me; it staggered my imagination when I heard the minister mention it, but my memory was not staggered, so I think I am right in that. That budget can be carried and fulfilled if we are but generous to people who are doing big things, instead of inflicting little pinpricks in their sides or their backs or their bellies. That is all these refusals amount to with respect to these little things. But one of these little things to a man engaged on the job may become a big thing by the time he reaches the end of his road. The income you are saving by this-what is a nice word?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Assistance to the oil industry.

Nonsense. I was going to use the word "puerile", but I thought that would be unkind; but what you are doing by this nonsense amounts to nothing in the economy of this country. When a man gets an oil well and an income, go after him; but for the love of all that is reasonable help him get that oil well producing. Do not hinder him, as you are doing by these refusals here, there, and elsewhere.
