speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, May 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gregg for the second reading of Bill No. 180, to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1946.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext:
This is one of those bills, Mr. Speaker, where one criticizes the government for their sins of omission rather than their sins of commission. The act does certain things which everyone in the house agrees with, but it fails to go far enough. It fails to take care of some inconsistencies and some needs which exist today. For instance the amount payable today under the War Veterans Allowance Act is just $40.41 per month. I do not think anyone will nrgue that is sufficient to meet the needs of an aged veteran. When this bill was passed in the first place, it was passed for the purpose of taking care of the prematurely aged war veterans who had served in the first war. The payments under it today certainly are not enough to do that. As a matter of fact, the government admitted that last year, by passing a special appropriation of $500,000, which was made available to take care of needy cases under this act. This year the minister has in the estimates an amount of $750,000 to take care of special cases of need.
It seems to me it would be far better if we were to increase the payments under the act rather than put on another means test, as we do under these special payments, and have the investigation which goes with it. If this bill had gone to a veterans affairs committee, it could have been discussed and we could have heard the submissions of the various veterans organizations in Canada with respect to this matter. There is another aspect of which we have not heard in connection with this matter. There is a lack
War Veterans Allowance Act of markets in Canada for certain products. As a matter of fact, there are two ministers of our government overseas today trying to find a market for surplus products which we have. I have no objection to seeking markets abroad providing we cannot find a market at home for those products. I think we are neglecting the market at home. If we provided an additional $10 per month to the prematurely aged veteran, I am sure that money would be spent in Canada to purchase many of the goods which are in surplus supply in this country today.
Instead of creating purchasing power at home, what are we doing? We are making loans or gifts to governments overseas so that they can purchase these products. It seems to me we would be much farther ahead if we first supplied these things to our own people. I am sure this is one way we could do it. There are many anomalies under the act. I know in my own constituency there are people who immigrated to this country from enemy countries after the first war, who are today receiving old age pensions. In the province of Saskatchewan they are getting more security under that old age pension than we are giving to our prematurely aged veterans of the first war under this act. It seems to me to be reasonable that the Department of Veterans Affairs should at least make the payments under the War Veterans Allowance Act equal to the best old age pension of any province in Canada; that is the least the government should do.
Then there is the matter of the widows of veterans who will be included under this amendment to the act. These will be the widows of veterans of the various wars which have been fought in the past. If the veteran lived in Canada for twenty years, his widow will be entitled to receive the war veterans allowance. If however the veteran died before completing his twenty years' residence in Canada, his widow will not receive the war veterans allowance. I feel sure there should be an amendment to the act to take care of these cases. There is also the matter of service in England to consider. For a number of years every veterans organization in Canada has been asking that service in England be considered for the purposes of the War Veterans Allowance Act, that is service in England during the first war. As time goes on, we are going to find that the veterans of the second world war will be entitled to the war veterans allowance for service in England, while the older veterans will not be entitled to it. As a matter of fact, we have cases today of men who served in both the first and the
2642	HOUSE OF
War Veterans Allowance Act second war, and who went to England. They are now entitled to the war veterans allowance. Their comrades who did not have the opportunity of serving in the second war are not entitled to that allowance. I feel that England should be declared a theatre of war for world war I. This would remove the anomaly under the act, and would place all veterans in the same position. These are just two or three things which I believe should be discussed further. That is one of the reasons why we in this group have insisted that we should have a permanent veterans affairs committee of the house before which we could take these different acts which have to do with veterans affairs, have them discussed, hear evidence from the various veterans organizations in the country, and come to some unanimous agreement as to the best treatment that we can give our veterans.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext:
There are just a few comments, Mr. Speaker, that I wish to make at this time. There is no doubt that the veterans organizations across Canada will be glad that at last we have granted entitlement to the war veterans allowance to former members of His Majesty's forces who fought prior to 1921 and who have been resident in Canada for twenty years or more. The act, however, goes beyond that and also includes former members of foreign powers who fought with us in the wars before 1921, but against us in the last war.
I am not opposing the proposal to make the war veterans allowance available to men of foreign powers, even though they may have fought against us in the last war. I feel, however, that before we bring in that group of men we should make more adequate provision for our own men who are receiving the war veterans allowance; and by that I mean that we should increase the amount of the war veterans allowance from $40 a month to $50 a month in order to put it on a level with what is paid under the Old Age Pensions Act in Alberta and British Columbia. But more especially I feel that the time has come when Britain should be declared a theatre of war in world war I.
We have made England a theatre of war in world war II, and I think the time has now come when England should be recognized as a theatre of war in the first war. After all, it is merely an arbitrary decision on the part of the government to declare that it was not a theatre of war. As a result of this amendment, it seems to me that we are going to have some undesirable situations in many communities. There will be veterans of Canada's armed forces who volunteered for overseas service in world war I, who may have


actually served three or four years overseas and who today may be 100 per cent incapacitated but yet are refused any benefits from the Department of Veterans Affairs on the ground that their service did not extend beyond England. Yet at the same time, as a result of this amendment, there will be veterans of foreign powers who fought with us in world war I but whose country fought against us in world war II, who have resided in this country for twenty years, and will now be eligible for the war veterans allowance; and they may be men whose physical condition may be far better than that of our own Canadians who are refused any help at all. That situation of course can only be taken care of by declaring England a theatre of war in world war I.
I think many people in districts throughout Canada are going to be somewhat disturbed when they see veterans of foreign powers that fought against us in the last war receiving the war veterans allowance when our own men are refused it. Mind you, I am not saying that these men fought against us in the last war but the country of which they are nationals fought against us. I realize that the act states that if these men fought with us in the first war and then fought against us in the second war, they will not get the benefits. But if their country fought against us in the second war they are apparently eligible. For instance, Italians who fought with us in the first war and yet whose country fought against us in the last war, I take it will be eligible for the benefits of this act even though they were interned during the last war. I take it that under this act. Japanese who fought with us in the first war and yet whose country fought against us in the second war will now be eligible for the benefits of the War Veterans Allowance Act. I think it will be a rather disturbing picture to many communities when they see our own men who volunteered for overseas service, who went overseas for three or four years, refused a pension merely because England was not declared a theatre of war. As I say,
I am not opposing the idea of the bonus of the war veterans allowance being paid to these men but I think that before that is paid we should more adequately take care of our own veterans.
I now wish to say just a few words with regard to the widows of veterans of His Majesty's forces who died before completing twenty years' residence in this country and who are thereby declared ineligible for the benefits of the act. I find it extremely hard to see any sense or reason for that ruling. So long as a veteran came to this country over twenty years ago and did not leave the

country, it seems to me that his death should not affect the granting of a pension to his widow, provided she has continued to live in this country since his death. Those are matters that I think should be given further consideration. I hope the minister can find it possible to refer this measure to a committee in order that these matters may be discussed, especially the matter to which I have referred with regard to nationals of foreign powers who fought with us in the first war and yet fought against us in the last war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext:
This whole question, Mr. Speaker, was dealt with at some length when the resolution preceding the bill was under consideration. I therefore have comparatively little further ground to cover tonight. At the outset I should like to support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), that this bill be sent to a committee. Throughout the session I have regretted that a special committee was not set up to deal with the problems of the veterans. But at the very least this bill should be sent to a committee, and I think such committee should be made up of veterans who are members of the house, just as has been the case in other sessions when we have had a special committee.
The bill is divided into two parts. One deals with the benefits which are now to be given to those imperials who settled in Canada up to the year 1930 and to other groups who served in other allied forces during the first war. Personally, I am greatly pleased that the imperials are at last to be made eligible for the war veterans allowance; but I urge upon the minister once more that a wider provision be made for the widows of these men. As he knows, we pointed out to him during the earlier discussions that it was unfair that all the widows should not be covered. Now we find, from the way in which the legislation reads, that the widow will not qualify unless her husband had been alive in Canada for twenty years. The test should be just the other way around. In other words, if he came here twenty years ago the widow should be eligible. Many of the widows came from the old country. In addition I imagine there would be quite a few who were native-born Canadians and who married imperial veterans. Neither group will be eligible unless the husband was actually alive for twenty years in Canada. I hope it is not yet too late to amend the legislation to cover both of these groups.
The second part of the bill deals with administration, in that for the first time it
War Veterans Allowance Act provides that committees shall be set up in the districts called district authorities. These district authorities are to exercise practically all of the powers that from 1930 to the present time have been exercised by the war veterans allowance board. I think that is a wise move, but it is a very drastic change in the handling of the war veterans allowances. That fact alone would justify the setting up of a committee, because there are many points which arise by virtue of the fact we are now to have these district authorities.
I hope that they will have power to review any case which has been dealt with in the past by the war veterans allowance board. Suppose a person has applied for war veterans allowance and has had his application rejected; I hope that it will now be possible for that veteran to apply to the district authority. The minister did not make that clear when he spoke on the earlier occasions. I would ask him to let us know whether the intention is that any veteran who has been turned down will now be able to apply to his district authority.
It also seems to me that the time has come to write into the War Veterans Allowance Act a benefit of the doubt section. There is such a section in the Pension Act numbered 63, which reads in this way:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant shall be entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which shall mean that it shall not be necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced, and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences and presumptions in favour of the applicant.
I suppose we have taken it for granted that the benefit of the doubt is being applied in the case of an application for war veterans allowance just as in the case of an application for pension. But it is not the law. Under the War Veterans Allowance Act there is no such benefit of the doubt clause. I have reached the conclusion personally that these ageing veterans will not get the kind of treatment to which the public believes they are entitled unless there is a benefit of the doubt clause written into the act.
When I spoke earlier I mentioned several types of cases, in which I thought there had been unfair decisions, and cases of that type would be covered if there were a benefit of the doubt clause. For example, the one that worries me the most is this question of the veteran who is under 60 years of age, or the widow who is under 55 years of age. In the War Veterans Allowance Act we find two provisions to cover them. In the first place

War Veterans Allowance Act if they are permanently unemployable because of physical or mental disability they can qualify, although they have not reached the age of 60 in the case of the veteran or 55 in the case of the widow. But then there is also this other provision: is incapable and unlikely to become capable of maintaining himself or herself because of economic handicaps combined with mental or physical disability or insufficiency.
I have always been of the opinion that that would cover practically every other case where the veteran was unable to earn his living; but within the last few months I have had two such cases brought to my attention which were decided against the applicant; one the case of a woman who qualified herself as a veteran, and the other the case of a widow both of whom I believe are unable to earn a living and are about 50 years of age. They cannot get work, and I do not consider that they are physically fit to work even if they could find a job, and yet it has been decided by the board that they do not come under either of those clauses. It may be that the board is correct in the strict interpretation of the act, but I know that was not the intention of members of parliament who served on the various veterans affairs committees. I believe these cases would be covered if there were a benefit of the doubt clause written into the act.
Other cases have to do with casual earnings. We thought that we had that casual earning provision broadened out to such an extent that anybody who had earnings which the ordinary person would consider were just odd amounts would not have those amounts counted against him in his application for an allowance. I doubt whether the board has been interpreting the provision in just such a wide way.
Then there are other instances. Perhaps you might call them borderline cases. But I do suggest that these borderline cases should get the benefit of the doubt. I would ask the minister to give consideration to putting in a benefit of the doubt clause which would make it clear beyond any question that parliament intended that borderline cases would be covered.
This change in the administration of the act also brings up another question, and it is this. A year ago an assistance fund was set up. The minister will correct me if I am wrong. I believe it is called the assistance-*

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext: The war veterans allowance assistance fund.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext:
-the war veterans allowance assistance fund, which, in effect, merely provided relief for war veterans allowance recipients who were drawing the full amount of allowance. It is of no use to a veteran

who is not drawing the full allowance. For example, I believe if he gets a pension of 25 per cent he cannot then get the full war veterans allowance and therefore would be ineligible for help under this fund, although actually he would not be getting any more than $40.41 if a single man; but because of the fact that he does not get it all in the form of war veterans allowance he does not qualify for help under the assistance fund. Furthermore it is only a vote; there is no legislation behind it; it depends on a vote being brought in each year, and that of course is a very uncertain and unstable way to provide for this help. There should be a statute providing for that assistance so that the rights of the veterans will be very clearly defined and that the help will not be subject merely to a parliamentary vote being brought in each year.
This assistance fund at the present time, although called a war veterans allowance assistance fund, is not being administered by the war veterans allowance board. It is administered by the welfare branch of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I would suggest that when these amendments become law, and we have the district authorities set up, such authorities should be given power to administer the assistance fund. That would seem to be more reasonable than having one group dealing with war veterans allowances and another group dealing with the assistance fund.
But the very fact that it has been necessary to set up an assistance fund and, in this year's vote, to increase it from $500,000 to $750,000, proves beyond the shadow of a doubt that the war veterans allowance itself is not ample, and that there should be an increase in the amount of war veterans allowance. If that were done, once the veteran had established a right to the war veterans allowance he or she would get an adequate amount; whereas at the present time the veteran gets only the old figure, and then has to go through a second means test every year in order to get help from this assistance fund- and he cannot get very much, at that. It is limited in the case of a single man to $10 a month and in the case of a married veteran to $15 a month, and as I have pointed out, unless he is getting full war veterans allowance, he cannot get any help at all under the assistance fund. You see, the cost of living is higher than it has ever been. The old age pensioners are getting more, in at least two of the provinces they are getting $10 a month more than the veteran can get; in fact, it means a good deal more than that in the case of the married

veteran. The single veteran in British Columbia gets $40 a month-to be exact it is $40.41-and the single old age pensioner gets $50.

If they are entitled to the dominion-provincial old age pension of $40, then the province adds $10 more. In fact, the province adds $10 even though they are not entitled to the full $40 under the dominion-provincial legislation. The province adds a bonus of $10, so that they are getting up to $50 a month. The veteran is properly a charge of the dominion government, just as the province has some responsibility in respect of the old age pensioner, and adds on $10 a month. It is an impossible situation when the veteran gets less than the old age pensioner in the province. I do suggest the time has long since passed when the war veterans allowance recipient should get the same amount as the old age pensioner.
I think the only way in which we will get this legislation made right is by referring it to a committee, allowing veterans organizations to make representations and giving the opportunity to members of the committee to question officers from the Department of Veterans Affairs and to go into this whole matter. If we do not do that it is very unlikely that there will be any legislation brought in at the next session in connection with the War Veterans Allowance Act. In fact, it might be quite impossible to get any further amendment to the act during the whole life of the present parliament. If we are to follow the course which has been followed by parliaments in Canada ever since the first war in dealing with veterans legislation as important as the bill before the house tonight, then we certainly should have a parliamentary committee. I hope the minister will agree to having such a committee set up, and to having this bill referred to that committee for study.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to touch briefly upon points made in earlier discussion both on the resolution and on the bill, but particularly those things affecting the bill itself. First may I refer to the observations of the hon. member for Kamloops as they are reported at page 1749 of Hansard, where he said:
I have had cases where ... it has .... taken months, in fact nearly a year, to complete a case ... to the final disposition.
It seems to me that no administration should take from six to nine months . . .
It may be that in cases requiring special investigation an inordinate length of time has been consumed but I am sure that hon. members know of their own personal knowledge that those are unusual cases. I will be the first to admit that in many cases it has taken too long to adjudge applications, and it is our sincere hope that the plan suggested here will help to shorten the time required.
At page 1752 of Hansard I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre shows a misapprehension about the payment of allowances when recipients of war veterans allowance are taken to hospital. He stated:
... I think it is a reasonable request that the wife of a veteran . . . who has to go to hospital, should get not less than she will get if she becomes a widow.
She does not get less under any circumstances. If a veteran is receiving $70 p.er month for himself and his wife, and he is admitted to hospital, usually about $15 is suspended leaving her with $55 which is more than she would receive if she were a widow.
The hon. member fbr Kings referred to a veteran who applied for war veterans allowance and was told that the expiry date for receiving such applications was in the year 1936. Of course that is untrue. There is no expiry date so far as war veterans allowance is concerned at the present time.
The hon. member for Calgary East referred to the supplementary allowances, and I should like to quote his exact words as recorded at page 1754 of Hansard. He said:
So far as I know, no one in that part of the country from which I come has received the benefit of that $10; no matter how desperate his circumstances may have been, he just did not get it.
In the Calgary district from which my friend comes supplementary allowance has been granted to 341 recipients out of 443 applicants. In short, more than 25 per cent of all those who receive war veterans allowance in the district have been receiving benefits from the assistance fund. I think those are the main points raised on the resolution and the bill. As to the point made by my hon. friend a few minutes ago about those


who will become eligible if the bill is put into effect, I am free to confess to the committee, Mr. Chairman, that after all the discussions of this matter going back for ten, twelve or fifteen years it was not until recently that anybody, even the veterans organizations themselves, got down to cases and said to themselves, "Where are we going to draw the line?" My hon. friend and I, among others, applauded loudly when my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and others talked about the peace of the world and better understanding between nations, about those who have come to Canada from other countries, have lived here for many years, and have taken part in the development of the country, and how we should begin to forget what their background was, what country they came from, their race or their creed. We have all thumped our desks and rightly so.
I am not going to go into detail on this question except to say that I would feel most unwilling to stand in the house and defend any other course than is reflected in the bill. In the case of those from across the Pacific who served with us in the first war, have been twenty years in Canada, and have taken part in the life of Canada, even with all the bitterness of feeling that has existed in the last ten years, I think we would be breaking down something if we did not treat them here in the same way as those who have come from the United Kingdom. I am the first to admit that I saw the difficulties referred to by my hon. friend. I suppose those things do occur in the administration of any such legislation. After all, we can only go step by step in these matters, keeping in step, if you like, with nineteen other departments of government. I am quite certain in the knowledge that progress is being made in the protection against hardship of those ageing veterans who have fought in battle, and that our people will understand if anomalies turn up here and there.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra referred to the benefit of the doubt. Frankly I had never thought of that in relation to the War Veterans Allowance Act. I think he will admit the Pension Act is a little different. Under that legislation doctors and lawyers have a go at it and there are certain very fine decisions to be made based upon opinions that are professional in nature. The factors surrounding the ageing veteran are not quite so professional. They are more rules of thumb. They are facts as to the living conditions under which the veteran is found, of trying to find out .these factors without being too much of a policeman in doing so, of trying to size them up and add them together and see whether or not they come within the spirit of the act.

I hope the cases he referred to can be reviewed again, but by and large I feel safe in saying that the benefit of the doubt has been put into practice in dealing with applications in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BENEFITS FOR CERTAIN FORMER MEMBERS OF FORCES OTHER THAN CANADIANS

Frankly I do not see any object in doing so. A question was asked whether a veteran who was in receipt of war veterans allowance in the past under the former method of administration will be able to have his case reviewed, or whether he can apply again if he was turned down in the past. Under the new plan the answer to that is yes. As my hon. friend knows, under war veterans allowance the man may apply as many times as he thinks he has a case.
The administration of the assistance fund has just passed through its first experimental year. So far as investigations are concerned they were conducted by those who had training in welfare work. They were not always employees of the Department of Veterans Affairs. Some of the investigations were conducted by trained social service workers within the community at the request of the department. It was done with the purpose of overcoming the charge that there is sometimes a second means test on top of a first. From my observation, in the main I think it has worked quite well.
As to referring the bill to a committee, in principle I can assure you at once that I
War Veterans Allowance Act have no objection. In practice, however, I cannot see the object. The points that have been made with respect to an increase in the basic rate at this time have been dealt with by myself this session, and I must repeat that I am not in a position to recommend an increase in the basic rate at this time. Consequently I can see no object in bringing that matter before a committee. I believe the points incorporated in this bill can be dealt with adequately in committee of the whole, which will give the board and those charged with the administration of the act an opportunity to put it into effect at the earliest possible moment.
Section stands.
